It is an Attic custom to designate the places themselves from the things in the place. Demosthenes in the speech Concerning the Trierarchy, and Lysias.
Deipnoforos ("dinner-bearer"). Hyperides, in the speech Against Demeas. It is also said that the "dinner-bearers" are now enrolled, because the mothers of the children shut away used to send in food to them each day at the temple of Athena, in which they lived, and themselves came together to greet their own children.
Deiradiotes. Deirades is a deme of the tribe Leontis, from which the demesman is Deiradiotes.
Deinoi. Used instead of "he will treat harshly" by Antiphon, On Truth, book two.
Dekazon ("bribing"). Isocrates, in the speech On the Peace. What this is, is clear to all. But Eratosthenes, in his work On the Old Comedy, shows whence the term comes, saying thus: "Lycus is a hero by the law-courts at Athens, having the form of the beast; before him those who took bribes used to turn, gathering in groups of ten (kata deka), whence the saying 'the ten of Lycus.'" Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says that Anytus first introduced the bribing of the law-courts.
Deka ("the Ten"). Deka and dekadouchos ("ten-holder"): Isocrates, in his special plea Against Callimachus: "for the Ten were in office, those established after the Thirty." Concerning the ten men elected at Athens after the dissolution of the Thirty, and what followed, Androtion has spoken in his third book. Each of these magistrates was called a "dekadouchos," as Lysias makes clear in the speech Concerning the Estate of Diogenes.
Dekadarchia ("rule of ten"). Isocrates. The historians constantly name the "decadarchies" established by the Lacedaemonians in the cities; but Isocrates, in the Panathenaicus, explained the word in a certain way, for he says that the Lacedaemonians made only ten men masters of each city. Philip, however, did not establish a decadarchy among the Thessalians, as is written in the sixth Philippic of Demosthenes, but a tetrarchy.
Dekateuein ("to tithe"). Demosthenes Against Androtion: "for not tithing them," instead of "exacting the tithe" and, as it were, "carrying off spoil"; for they used to tithe to the gods the things taken from the enemy. But when Demosthenes, in the speech Against Medon, speaking of a certain maiden, says thus, "not to tithe her nor to initiate her," Didymus the grammarian, who wrote a book about this, says that Lysias, in the speech On Behalf of the Daughter of Phrynichus, used "to tithe" for "to serve as a bear." "To tithe," he says, was properly used of "to consecrate," since it was a Greek custom to consecrate to the gods the tithes of the surplus. Perhaps, then, the orator used "to tithe" for "to serve as a bear," since the girls of ten served as bears.
Dekateutas ("tithe-collectors"). Used instead of "tax-farmers, those who collect the tithe," by Antiphon in his Defense Against the Indictment of Demosthenes. That the tithe was a customs-due, Demosthenes has shown in his speech On the Immunities.
Dekatelogous ("tithe-collectors"). Those who collect the tithe—the same, then, as the "dekateutai." Demosthenes Against Aristocrates.
Dekeleikos ("Decelean"). The Peloponnesian War, named from a part of its later stage.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Delfinion. A place in Chios, as Thucydides says in his eighth book. There is another Delphinium at Athens, a shrine of Apollo, where the law-court "at the Delphinium" was also located; Demosthenes in the speech Against Boeotus.
Derkulidas. A king of the Lacedaemonians.
Dermatikon ("hide-money"). Lycurgus in the work entitled An Account of His Public Administration. By "dermatikon" the orator would mean the money accruing from the hides that were sold.
Dermestes ("hide-eater"). Lysias, in the speech Against Eupeithes. Didymus, in the seventh book of his Doubtful Words, says that this is the term Sophocles uses in the Niobe for the worm; but Aristarchus, explaining the passage in Sophocles, took it to mean the snake. Perhaps, rather, the "dermestes" would be whatever eats hides, as is also suggested in the sixth book of the Milesian Tales of Aristides.
Deusopoios ("fast-dyeing"). Properly the word is used of purple that has a lasting and unfading bloom of dye; but by metaphor it is applied by the ancients to all other things that have a lasting and durable color, as Plato too makes clear in the fourth book of the Republic. Diphilus in the Foster-Brothers: "there is a good dyer in the child; for he has shown us these swaddling-clothes to be altogether fast-dyed."
Demainetos. A proper name.
Deliastai. Those who went out to Delos as sacred envoys; Lycurgus Against Menesaechmus.
Demarchos ("demarch"). Lysias, in the speech Against Moschus. The demarch was a kind of magistrate; these officials made the registrations of the lands in each deme. Further, the deme-registers were in their keeping, and they convened the demes whenever there was need, and gave the vote to them. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says these were established by Cleisthenes, having the same charge as the naucraries before them. That the demarchs took pledges, Aristophanes shows in the Women Seizing the Tents.
Demokoinos ("public torturer"). The public examiner under torture. Isocrates, in the Trapeziticus, has more or less explained the word.
Demopoietos ("made a citizen"). One who is a foreigner by nature but has been made a citizen by the people. In what manner some become "demopoietoi," Demosthenes has shown in his speech Against Neaera, if it is genuine.
Demosios ("public slave"). Demosthenes in the Philippics. They call the slaves of the city "demosioi." Aeschines Against Timarchus: "a public man, a household-slave of the city."
Demotele ("publicly maintained"). Demotele and demotika hiera ("public rites and deme rites"): these differed both from one another and from the rites of the orgeones and the clans, as Dinarchus shows in his speech Against Stephanus.
Demoteuomenos ("registered in a deme"). "To be registered in a deme" is to share in a particular deme and to conduct business from it; Antiphon in his Defense Against Philip, if it is genuine.
Demofanes. A proper name.
Diagoreuon ("speaking at variance"). Isaeus, in the speech Against Diocles, uses "diagoreuon" in a special sense, instead of "saying different and not the same things." For "diagoreuein" is the opposite, among these writers, of "synagoreuein" ("to agree"), just as "to be carried along with" is opposed to "to be at variance," and "to share in citizenship" to "to be at political odds," and "to be in harmony" to "to be in discord."
Diagramma ("schedule"). Hyperides, in the speech Against Epicles. The amount fixed in the symmories for how much each man must contribute. It was not the same amount for all, but according to the assessment of property. Concerning these matters Hyperides has shown most clearly in his speech Against Polyeuctus, Concerning the Schedule. The "diagrapheus," moreover, is the man appointed in the symmories to determine how much each man ought to contribute, as the same author again makes clear in his speech Against Polyeuctus.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Diagrafe ("specification"). The description of the mines being sold, showing by writing from what starting-point to what limit it is sold.
Diagrapsasthai ("to have the charge struck out"). Lysias, in the speech Against Nicides, if it is genuine, used instead of "to cancel the charge."
Diadoseis ("distributions"). The shares falling due from an equal division; Lysias.
Diakechremenon ("lent out in parts"). Used instead of "lent out piecemeal" by Demosthenes Against Aphobus.
Diastasis ("arrangement"). Antiphon, On Truth, book two: "concerning the arrangement (diastasis) now prevailing," instead of "the ordering of the whole."
Diagrapsantos ("having paid down"). Dinarchus Against Lycurgus. Perhaps instead of "having paid in and deposited." But some take it instead of "having reckoned out through the bank," as we say in common speech.
Diathesis ("disposal, arrangement"). Used instead of "sale" by Isocrates in the Busiris. Antiphon, in the speech Against the Information of Callias, said "diethemetha" instead of "we sold"; and the same author, in his work On Concord, uses it instead of "management": "but knowing the management (diathesis), they listen." Phrynichus, in the Tragic Actors, says "by the arrangement (diathesis) of the verses." For they also use the verb "diathesthai" for "to manage"; Antiphon, On Truth, book one: "but stripped of resources, it would manage (diathoito) many fine things badly." "Diathesthai" used instead of "to make an agreement," Hyperides Against Demosthenes.
Dialexis ("allotment-division"). "Dialanchanein" is to divide by lot, and "dialexis" is the act; Antiphon in the speech Against Philinus.
Dia mesou teichous ("through the middle wall"). Antiphon Against Nicocles. There being three walls in Attica, as Aristophanes too says in the Triphales—the northern, the southern, and the Phaleric—the southern was called the "middle" wall, since it lay between the other two; Plato also mentions it in the Gorgias.
Diacheirotonia ("voting by show of hands"). The decision of a vote taken by show of hands in a multitude; Demosthenes both in the speech Against Timocrates and Against Androtion.
Diamemetremene emera ("the measured-out day"). There is a measure of water flowing in proportion to a measured interval of the day; it was measured out in the month Posideon. To this the greatest men, and in the greatest causes, contended. The water was divided into three parts: one for the prosecutor, one for the defendant, and the third for the jurors. These matters the orators themselves have set forth most clearly, as also Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon; and Aristotle teaches about them in the Constitution of the Athenians. But one must consider the passage in Isaeus, in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes, where, though the day was measured out, he says at one point that the trials took place without water, at another that they took place by the water-clock.
Diametron ("short measure"). The deficiency from the just measure; Dinarchus in the information Against Callisthenes.
Diaskeuasasthai. Used instead of "to equip oneself" by Isaeus in the speech Against Callicrates.
Diaseistous ("the shaken-down"). Aeschines Against Timarchus. They seem to be named from being moved and shaken down first, and then cast away, that they might be more free from harm; Menander in the Men for Sale.
Diapsefisis ("scrutiny by vote"). Used in a special sense of the examinations in the demes, which take place concerning each of the deme-members, whether he is truly a citizen and demesman, or has been smuggled in, being a foreigner; Aeschines Against Timarchus. Most fully Androtion, in his Atthis, and Philochorus, in the sixth book of the Atthis, have discoursed about the scrutinies, as they took place in the archonship of Archias.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Diamarturia ("counter-deposition"). Diamarturia and diamarturein: the "diamarturia" was a kind of special plea; for before the suit was brought into court, it was permitted to anyone who wished to depose that the suit was, or was not, admissible. It differs from the special plea in that the "diamarturia" is made not only by the defendants but also by the prosecutors. And formerly it was open to the prosecutor to put forward someone deposing that the suit was admissible, and the trial took place first concerning this, against the man who made the deposition, not against the original litigant; and if the prosecutor did not put forward a witness, then it was open to the defendant to bring forward someone deposing that the suit was not admissible, and again the contest was against the man who made the deposition. They were liable to charges of false testimony in the counter-depositions as well, just as in ordinary depositions; Lysias in the counter-deposition Against Aristodemus, if the speech is genuine. Isaeus, in the speech Against Python for Desertion, says that foreigners cannot make a counter-deposition; but Hyperides, in his speech Against Aristagoras for Being Without a Patron, book two, says that the laws bid anyone who wishes to make a counter-deposition in the indictments for being without a patron, foreigners and natives alike. Perhaps, then, in the suits of desertion foreigners are forbidden to make counter-depositions, but in those of being without a patron they are not forbidden. Dinarchus, however, has used "to make a counter-deposition" not of the man who himself deposed, but of the man who furnished someone to make a counter-deposition in the counter-deposition concerning the non-adjudicability of the daughter of Aristophon. And this orator, in the speech Against Hedyle, describes the manner of the counter-deposition.
Diaitetai ("arbitrators"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Meidias. The arbitrators are distinct from the jurors; for the latter gave judgment in appointed courts and decided the appeals from the arbitrators, while the arbitrators—either chosen by lot beforehand or appointed by the litigants who entrusted their case to them—arbitrated for the parties. And if it satisfied the litigants, the suit was at an end; but if not, then, having cast the charges, the challenges, the depositions, and also the laws and the other proofs of each party into urns and sealed them, they handed them over to the introducers of suits. Aristotle speaks about them in the Constitution of the Athenians.
Diasuesai. Used instead of "to throw into confusion" and, as it were, "to make impossible" by Antiphon in his speech Concerning the Revolution; Menander in the Widow: "let him with shouting make the city distracted (diastaton)."
Didaskalos ("teacher, producer"). In a special sense they call "teachers" the composers of dithyrambs or of comedies or of tragedies. Antiphon, in his speech Concerning the Chorus-Member, says: "I obtained Pantacles as producer"; for that Pantacles was a poet, Aristotle has shown in the Productions. The word is frequent also in the old comedy in this sense.
Diegguesin ("provision of sureties"). Used instead of "the furnishing of sureties" by Demosthenes Against Timocrates. But in the speech Against Neaera, if it is genuine, he says: "having been bailed (diegguetheisa) by Stephanus."
Diekodonise. Demosthenes, in the speech On the Embassy, used instead of "he tested and examined thoroughly." The metaphor is either from those who patrol the watches at night with bells, as Euripides in the Palamedes, or from those who test fighting-quails by the sound of a bell, as Aristarchus says.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Di eniautou ("through the year"). Used instead of "through the whole year" by Antiphon, Concerning the Tribute of the Lindians. Teleclides, in the Prytaneis, said "through the day" (di hemeras) instead of "through the whole day."
Diespeusamen. Used instead of "I made with zeal," or instead of "I accomplished," by Isaeus in the speech Against Hermon, Concerning a Pledge.
Dieskarifesametha. Isocrates in the Areopagiticus. "To scratch over" (skariphesasthai) is to do something carelessly and not with the proper precision.
Dieteinanto. In a special sense Antiphon applied this in his speech Concerning the Murder of Herodes, instead of "they denied with strained earnestness."
Diellaxen. Used instead of "he changed his life, he died," by Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess.
Dierxa. Used instead of "I held office continuously to the end" by Lysias in his Defense on the Indictment of Mixidemus.
Diipoleia. A certain festival at Athens, the Diipoleia; Antiphon in his speech Concerning the Chorus-Member.
Dikaiogenes. This man was a writer of tragedies. He also composed dithyrambs.
Dikaiopolis. Lysias, in the speech Against Thrasybulus, if it is genuine. A city in Thrace near Abdera. Perhaps there is also some other Dikaiopolis.
Dikaiosis ("a claim of right, a punishment"). Lysias, in the speech On Behalf of the Soldier, if it is genuine, says "and the claims of right (dikaioseis) very much," instead of "pleas of justice." But Thucydides often uses "dikaiosis" for "punishment."
Dike ("private suit"). The word has other meanings as well, but in a special sense it is used of private charges, as Demosthenes makes clear in his speech Against Conon.
Dioikiein ("to settle apart"). Used instead of "to separate, so that not all dwell in the same place, but apart and severally," by Demosthenes in the fifth book of the Philippics.
Diopeuon ("inspecting"). Demosthenes, in the speech Against Lacritus. "Diopos" is the term for the man who manages and oversees the affairs of a ship, the one we call the "supercargo."
Diotimos. A proper name, an admiral of the Athenians.
Diofantos. A proper name.
Dioaugion ("very great"). Isaeus, in the speech Against Stratocles: "very great matters (diolygia)," instead of "great." And Plato too uses it.
Diomosia ("oath of both parties"). Properly the oath taken by the litigants; Demosthenes Against Aristocrates.
Dokimastheis ("having been approved"). Used instead of "having been enrolled among the men" by Demosthenes in the speech Against Onetor. But "to be approved" (dokimasthenai) is also used of magistrates, as the same orator makes clear in the appeal Against Eubulides. It was also used of public men, even if they held no office at all; for their life was sometimes examined, as Aeschines says in the speech Against Timarchus. Lycurgus, in the speech On the Administration, says: "there are three scrutinies (dokimasiai) according to the law: one by which the nine archons are examined, another by which the orators, and a third by which the generals." He mentions also, in the same speech, the scrutiny of the cavalry.
Doriskos. A place in Thrace; Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon, and Herodotus.
Dosis ("gift, deed of gift"). In a special sense, among the orators, it is the contract drawn up when someone gives his own property to another through the magistrates, as in Dinarchus.
Drakontides. One of the Thirty. Hyperides.
Drakon. This man was a most distinguished lawgiver, as Aeschines says. There is another Draco whom Isocrates mentions in the Panegyricus.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Drggilon. A Thracian place; Demosthenes in the Philippics.
Dromokerukes ("running heralds"). Aeschines. Those called day-runners.
Drumos. A city between Boeotia and Attica; Demosthenes in the speech On the Embassy. Aristotle, in his Justifications, says thus: "then a Drymus, one Attic and the other Boeotian."
Drus. Demosthenes Against Aristocrates. A city in Epirus. There is also another in Thrace, which the orator now mentions; this one Theopompus, in his twenty-sixth book, says was settled by Iphicrates.
Dusanios ("hard to please"). Antiphon. The man vexed at everything, even at what is small and contemptible. Hippocrates too somewhere used the word, and Menander.
Dusaules. Dinarchus in the adjudication concerning the Priestess, if it is genuine. Asclepiades, in the fourth book of his Subjects of Tragedy, says that Dysaules was autochthonous, and that, having lived with Baubo, he had children, Protonoe and Nisa. But Palaephatus, in the ninth book of his Trojan History, says that he, together with his wife, received Demeter.
Dusopoumai ("I am abashed"). Used instead of "I fear" by Demosthenes in the Philippics, and by Xenophon in the second book of the Memorabilia.
Dorieus. The name of a pancratiast.
Doroxenia ("bribery for citizenship"). Lysias, in the speech Against Nicides. Hyperides explained the word in his speech Against Aristagoras, writing thus: "since the law on bribery-for-citizenship (doroxenia) too is fitting to be brought to bear on the present case; for if he has said that those acquitted of an alien-status charge may be indicted again by anyone who wishes, should they appear not to have been justly acquitted the first time, how is it not plain that the right lies against Aristagoras?" And Aristotle too, in the Constitution of the Athenians, speaking of the thesmothetai, writes thus: "there are also indictments before them, for which a deposit is laid down, of alien status and of bribery-for-citizenship, if someone, by giving bribes, escapes the charge of malicious prosecution."
Doron grafe ("indictment for bribery"). Whenever one of the public men was charged with taking bribes, the charge against him was expressed in two ways: "bribe-taking" (dorodokia) and "indictment for bribes" (doron graphe). Dinarchus, then, entitled one speech "Against Polyeuctus for Bribery," but in the speech "Against Pytheas for Alien Status" he often names the indictment for bribes.
5. Ean tis grapsamenos me ("if anyone who has brought an indictment..."). If anyone who has brought an indictment does not obtain a fifth part of the votes, he incurs a fine of a thousand drachmas, and a certain loss of civic rights is added. Lysias, in the speech On Behalf of the Law Against the Orators, has discoursed about these matters, and Theophrastus in his work On the Laws.
Hebdomeuomenou ("when the seventh day was being kept"). Lysias in the speech Against Eteocles, Concerning Money, if it is genuine. For newborn children they used to keep the seventh and the tenth days, and they gave them their names—some on the seventh, as the orator too says, others on the tenth. Aristotle, in the ninth book of the History of Animals, writes thus: "most of them die before the seventh day; for which reason they then give the names, in the confidence that they will now survive."
Eggutheke ("a stand"). A certain speech is current, ascribed to Lysias, entitled Concerning the Stand. It would be a vessel suitable for setting mixing-bowls or basins or something of the sort upon it, as Callixenus suggests in the fourth book of his work On Alexandria, and Daimachus the Plataean in the second book of his work On India.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Hedoliasai ("to make benches"). Lycurgus in the work entitled An Account of His Public Administration, used of fitting out the benches. And the "hedolia" are the seats in the ships; Herodotus, book one.
Ethnos ("class, nation"). Not only the great and populous race, but in a special sense a certain part of the city. Demosthenes, in his speech Against Aristocrates: "if someone should ask you what you consider the most worthless of all the classes (ethne) in the city, you would name neither the farmers nor the merchants nor those from the silver-mines nor any of such men." And in the ninth Philippic he says: "but how does Thessaly stand? Has he not taken away their cities and their constitutions and set up tetrarchies among them, so that they may be enslaved not only by cities but also by nations (ethne)?"
Eiloteuein ("to be a helot"). To be a slave; Isocrates in the Panegyricus. For the "helots" are not the slaves of the Lacedaemonians by birth, but the first who were subdued of those inhabiting the city of Helos, as many others testify, and Hellanicus in his first book.
Eisaggelia ("impeachment"). It is the name of a certain public suit, and there are three kinds of impeachments. One concerns the greatest public wrongs that admit of no delay, and for which neither a magistracy has been established nor laws laid down for the magistrates to introduce them, but the first proceeding is taken before the Council or the people; and for which, if the defendant is convicted, the greatest penalties are imposed, while the prosecutor, if he does not win, suffers no penalty—except if he does not obtain a fifth part of the votes; for then he pays a thousand drachmas. In old times these men too were more severely punished. Another impeachment is for ill-treatment; these are brought before the archon, and they entail no penalty for the prosecutor, even if he does not obtain a fifth part of the votes. There is yet another impeachment against arbitrators; for if anyone was wronged by an arbitrator, it was permitted to impeach him before the jurors, and on conviction he was disfranchised. Isaeus, however, in his speech Concerning the Estate of Hagnias, called the same matter both an impeachment and an indictment.
Eis emfanon katastasin ("for the production of property in open view"). It is the name of a suit, for having the disputed property in the open; Isaeus in the speech Concerning the Estate of Philoctemon. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says that this suit is brought before the archon, and that the examining magistrate introduces it into court.
Eis en elthen ("it came to one"). Used instead of "it was brought into agreement."
Eisepodizon. Used instead of "they were entering the land on foot" by Isaeus in the speech Against the Orgeones.
Eis eo ("at dawn"). Used instead of "toward the breaking day" by Isaeus in the speech Concerning the Estate of Ciron.
Eisfresein. Used instead of "to bring in, to admit," by Antiphon and Demosthenes in the eighth Philippic. The word is frequent in the old comedy.
Ekalistroun. Demosthenes in the speech Against Euergus and Mnesibulus, if it is genuine. It is an Ionic word, and perhaps the speech may be by Dinarchus; for he too uses foreign words.
Hekates nesos ("the island of Hecate"). Lycurgus Against Menesaechmus. Before Delos lies a small island, which by some is called Psammetiche, as Phanodemus says in his first book. Semus, in the first book of his Deliaca, says it was called Psammetiche because the goddess was honored with offerings of meal-cakes (psammeta); the "psammeta" are a kind of cake.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Hekatombaion ("Hecatombaeon"). The name of a month. Hyperides. Ammonius, at any rate, says it was called so from the fact that most hecatombs were sacrificed in this month.
Hekatomnos. A proper name.
Hekatompedon ("the Hundred-Footer"). Lycurgus in the work entitled An Account of His Public Administration. The Parthenon was called by some "Hecatompedon" on account of its beauty and good proportion, not on account of its size, as Menecles or Callicrates says in the work On Athens.
Ekdeia ("deficiency"). Hyperides, in the speech Against Pasicles: "but if there be any deficiency," that is, "if there be any shortfall of the money previously available."
Ekdexamenos ("having taken up"). Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "having taken up and proposed." "To take up" (ekdexasthai) is, having received from another, to undertake the matter oneself in the second place. But one must consider how the passage in the fifth Philippic, spoken by the orator, stands: "and the seeming to have taken up the things done by those men."
Ekdikasasthai ("to exact by a fresh suit"). To exact afresh by means of a suit; Isaeus in the speech Against Callicrates.
Ekdosis ("a putting-out"). The maritime loan, as it were "a giving out" (exo dosis); Demosthenes Against Aphobus, book one.
Ekkleteuein ("to compel attendance"). To bring into court, that someone may be compelled to give testimony; Aeschines in his Defense on the Embassy.
Eklogeis ("collectors"). Those who collect and exact the debts owed to the public treasury. Antiphon, in his work Concerning the Tribute of the Samothracians: "for there were chosen among us as collectors those who seemed to have the most property." Lysias, in the speech Against Aresandrus: "but now we register everything with the collectors of the tribute."
Eklozete. Demosthenes Against Meidias. They called the noise made in the mouth a "klosmos," which they used for the driving off of the performances they did not gladly hear.
Ekmarturia ("deposition by proxy"). It differs from the ordinary deposition in that the deposition is of those present, but the "ekmarturia" is of those absent. Most clearly Demosthenes teaches about these matters in the speech Against Stephanus, and Dinarchus in the speech On Behalf of Aeschines Against Deinias.
Ek periousias ("out of abundance"). Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "but this man accuses me out of abundance." It is better to understand it thus: that I am in the utmost peril, but he accuses me out of his great superfluity—not concerning money, as some suppose.
Ekplintheusas. Used instead of "having dissolved and taken out the bricks" by Isaeus in the speech Against Diocles.
Ekpolemosai ("to provoke to war"). Demosthenes in the Philippics, used instead of "to bring into a state of war," as also often in Thucydides. In the Atticianus copies, however, it is written with an eta, as also in Xenophon in the sixth book of the Hellenica.
Ek proagoges ("from compulsion"). Used instead of "by necessity and not from nature nor simply." The metaphor is from those not at rest, but forced forward from their barriers by bonds. Demosthenes Against Aristocrates.
Ekfulloforesai ("to vote out by leaves"). If one of the councillors seemed to be doing wrong, the Council voted about him whether he ought no longer to be a councillor. Instead of voting-pebbles they used leaves, by which each marked his own decision. Dinarchus, in the speech Against Polyeuctus, "when he had been voted out by leaves."
Elaious. A city in the Thracian Chersonese.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Elateia. Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon; it was the greatest of the cities among the Phocians. From the orator again, in the seventh book of the Philippics, if it is genuine, these words: "in Cassopia, three cities, Pandosia and Bucheta and Elateia." It must be said that it is better written in some copies with a rho, "Elatreia"; for Theopompus, at any rate, in his forty-third book, says there are four cities of the Cassopaeans, and not three as Demosthenes says—Elatreia and Pandosia and Bitia and Bucheta.
Elafrotatous ("most light, gentle"). The ancients use the word in a good sense too, instead of "most gentle," as the opposite of "most grievous and most oppressive." Isocrates in the Panathenaicus: "rendering themselves as light and as moderate as possible to their associates."
Eleokopon ("marsh-cutters"). Lysias in the speech Against Demosthenes for Maladministration of a Guardianship: "spending five months in company with the marsh-cutters." By "marsh-cutters" the orator would mean those who cut the marshes (hele), with an epsilon inserted, as "marsh-grown parsley" in Homer. Perhaps, however, the name comes from the "eleon," which is a wooden vessel. Aristophanes in the Knights: "if he should take down the eleon against me."
Eleutherios Zeus ("Zeus the Liberator"). Hyperides: "to Zeus, then, gentlemen of the jury, the surname of being called 'Liberator' came because the freedmen built the stoa near him." But Didymus says the orator is mistaken; for he was called "Liberator" because the Athenians were delivered from the Persians. That he is inscribed as "Savior" but is also named "Liberator," Menander too makes clear.
Eleusinia. Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Callippus. To the victors at the Eleusinia a prize was given. The city Eleusis was named after Eleusinus the son of Hermes. Others give other causes and say that the Eleusinia is only a festival.
Helikteres ("spiral earrings"). A kind of earring; Lysias.
Helixos. One of the distinguished men among the Megarians.
Hellanodikai ("the Hellanodikai"). Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Callippus, against the Eleans. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Eleans, says that the Eleans at first established one Hellanodikes, but after the passage of time two, and at the last nine. But Aristodemus the Elean says that those who conducted the contest at the last were ten Hellanodikai, one from each tribe.
Hellenotamiai ("the Hellenic treasurers"). Andocides in the speech On the Peace, if it is genuine. That the Hellenotamiai were a magistracy who administered the moneys, Aristotle too makes clear in the Constitution of the Athenians. Thucydides too mentions them in his first book.
Embeblemena ("grafted things"). Used instead of "things grafted in" by Demosthenes in his speech Against Nicostratus. And Aristotle calls such pears "grafted ones."
Hembios ("living"). Antiphon, On Truth, book one: "and the rot of the wood may become living (embios)," instead of "in life," that is, "may live and not be dried up nor die."
Embrachu ("in brief"). Used instead of "simply and in summary" by Antiphon.
Emmenoi dikai ("monthly suits"). Both the commercial suits and those concerning loan-clubs; Demosthenes and Hyperides.
Empodon ("in the way"). Antiphon, in his speech Concerning the Revolution: "and you punished those in the way (empodon)," instead of "those who fell in," as also Andocides in the speech Against Alcibiades.
Empousa. Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon. They say it is a certain apparition of Hecate, which appeared to the unfortunate. The comedy is full of the word.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Henai archai ("the bygone magistracies"). The past ones; Demosthenes Against Aristogiton.
Endeixis ("information"). A kind of public suit, under which they brought those debarred by the laws from certain places or actions, if they did not keep away from them. There are many speeches of information, but the best known are those of Demosthenes Against Aristogiton.
Endekazontas. Used instead of "celebrating, holding the tenth-day feast among themselves," by Demosthenes in his speech Against Theocrines.
En Diomeiois Erakleion ("the Heracleum in Diomeia"). Hyperides Against Conon. The comic poets too mention the festival held in honor of Heracles in Diomeia.
Enepiskemma ("counter-claim"). Enepiskemma and enepiskepsasthai: Demosthenes in the speech Against Timotheus. Whenever someone's property was confiscated, it was permitted to the man claiming to be a creditor of that person to come forward and say that a debt was owed him in the property. There is also a certain speech entitled Of Demosthenes, Against Critias, Concerning the Counter-Claim, which Callimachus records as genuine, but Dionysius of Halicarnassus as falsely ascribed.
Eneskeuasmenen. Isaeus, in the speech Against Aristogiton and Archippus, used instead of "fitted out and forged."
Enetimato. Demosthenes in the speech Against Spudias. "Apetimato" differs from "enetimato": for when someone takes a security against a certain sum of money, he is said "to value back" (apotimasthai); but when someone reckons a part of the money in certain articles, this is said as "he valued it in" (enetimesato).
Hene kai nea ("the old and new day"). Hyperides in the speech Against Hygiaenon. The day we call the thirtieth, the Athenians call "old and new," from its having the end of the former month and the beginning of the latter. Polemon says that the Athenians once called it "Demetrias" in honor of Demetrius the Macedonian. "Enen" and "eis enen" they use for "the day after tomorrow." And in general "enon," with the rough breathing, means the former and bygone.
Enthrupta ("crumb-cakes"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. Didymus the grammarian, in his commentary on the speech, having said that "enthrypta" are something obvious and well known from the very word, sets out a more elaborate and unattested explanation; the "enthrypta" are things made of pastry, or foods broken in (enthrybomena). Some associate them with the mysteries; and Apollo too among the Athenians is called "Enthryptos."
En limnais Dionusion ("the Dionysium in the Marshes"). Isaeus, Concerning the Estate of Ciron. There is a place at Athens called Limnae ("Marshes"), in which Dionysus is honored.
Enneakrounon ("the Nine-Spouts"). Isocrates in the speech On the Exchange of Property. A certain spring at Athens; it was formerly called Callirrhoe.
Ennea odoi ("Nine Ways"). Aeschines in his Defense on the Embassy. A place in Thrace near Amphipolis.
En parabustoi ("in a corner"). Used instead of "secretly and not openly" by Hyperides in the speech Against Archestratides.
Ensemainomenos. Used instead of "showing and revealing" by Isocrates.
En freattoi ("at Phreatto"). Demosthenes, in his speech Against Aristocrates, has gone through accurately the court at Phreatto, speaking thus: "Consider, then, yet a fifth court, of what sort, surpassing that at Phreatto. Here, men of Athens, the law bids one stand trial if a man, having gone into exile for an involuntary act, before those who banished him have relented, is charged with another, voluntary, homicide." And a little later he says: "he brought the judges to a place where it was possible to approach that man, having appointed a certain spot of the country at Phreatto, called so, on the sea; then the one comes sailing in a boat and speaks, not touching the land, while the others listen and judge on the land. And if he is convicted, he has paid the just penalty for voluntary homicide; but if he is acquitted, he is let off from this charge, but undergoes exile for the other homicide." The court seems to have been named after a certain hero Phreatto, as Theophrastus says in the sixteenth book of his Laws.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Exagistos ("accursed"). Used instead of "exceedingly polluted and full of curse." Aeschines, in the speech Against Ctesiphon, used the word of a certain harbor.
Exaireseos dike ("suit for removal"). Whenever someone led another off as a slave, and then someone removed him as a free man, it was permitted to the man laying claim to the person as a slave to bring a suit for removal against the man removing him into freedom; Isaeus in the speech On Behalf of Eumathes, for the Recovery of Freedom.
Exarasasthai ("to fulfill the prayers"). Aeschines Against Ctesiphon: "that he dedicated golden shields to the new temple before fulfilling the prayers (exarasasthai)." "Exarasasthai" is to complete the "arai," that is, the prayers, which they were accustomed to make at the foundations of temples.
Exegguesis. The releasing of someone through the provision of sureties; Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates.
Exenize ("he spoke as a foreigner"). Demosthenes in the appeal Against Eubulides: "for they have slandered my father as though he spoke as a foreigner (exenize)." Perhaps it means "he was a foreigner," and not, as Didymus says, "he did not speak in the Attic way, but in a foreign manner."
Exepremnizon. Used instead of "they cut down the stumps," that is, the trunks down to the roots, by Demosthenes in his speech Concerning the Estate of Hagnias.
Exetazesthai. Used instead of "to be seen" by Demosthenes Against Stephanus. And in the speech Against Androtion he says "you were examined (exetasthes)," instead of "you were seen, you were beheld."
Exegetes ("expounder"). Isaeus, in the speech Concerning the Estate of Ciron. The man who expounds sacred matters. There were also things, customary toward the departed, which they expounded to those who needed them. Demosthenes too, in the speech Against Euergus and Mnesibulus, makes this clear, often naming the expounders in the plural.
Exekestos. A proper name; Demosthenes Against Aristocrates.
Exorchesamenos ("having danced it away"). Used instead of "having fled and run off" by Demosthenes in his speech Against Androtion, who said it in jest at the same time, on account of the procession of the Dionysia.
Exoules ("of ejectment"). The name of a suit which those who say they are kept from their own property bring against those who keep them out. The name comes from "exillein," which is "to thrust out and cast out." Suits of ejectment are brought, with the penalties, by those who do not recover their own within the proper term, when the condemned have become overdue. Those convicted of ejectment gave to the successful party what they had taken from him, and paid to the treasury the value assessed. A creditor too was sued for ejectment if he tried to hold a piece of property of his debtor and was prevented by someone. And if anyone was kept from cultivation, the law grants a suit of ejectment against the one keeping him out. And concerning a slave too, and everything of which one says it belongs to him. These matters Isaeus teaches clearly, and Lysias in the speech Against Stratocles for Ejectment. Dinarchus, however, in the adjudication of the Croconidae, has used the term "ejectment" in a special sense, of the priestess who would not perform her own duties. That the name is applied to everything from which one is cast out of his own property, and not, as Caecilius thinks, only to those owing in consequence of a condemnation, Phrynichus too makes clear in the Grass-Cutters.
Exomosia ("oath of disclaimer"). The denying of some action on oath, on account of sickness or some other pretext, as Demosthenes makes clear in the speech On the Embassy.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Epaggelia ("notice, denunciation"). It has other meanings too, but in a special sense it is used of those who charge another with speaking and taking part in public life when it is not permitted, and it is, as it were, a "notice"; Aeschines Against Timarchus. Among these writers "to give notice" (epaggellesthai) is also used instead of "to command" or "to demand," as in Antiphon, in his work Concerning the Tribute of the Lindians, and in Demosthenes, in the speech On the Embassy.
Epaktos orkos ("the imported oath"). One which a man voluntarily takes upon himself, that is, chooses; but others say the opposite, that it is one imported from elsewhere, and not self-chosen. Lysias in the speech Against Chaerestratus, and Isocrates of Apollonia in his Exhortations to Demonicus. There are three kinds of oath: the oath of denial, the oath of affirmation, and the so-called "imported" oath. This last is not simple; for the man put forward by the one administering the oath must answer back to him in the very same words.
Epaktrokeles. Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus. It is a kind of boat, having its construction compounded of a fishing-skiff (epaktris) and a yacht (keles). It was generally a pirate-craft, as Dinarchus too says in the scrutiny Against Polyeuctus.
Epallaxeis ("interchanges"). Used instead of "dealings or minglings" by Antiphon, On Truth, book one.
Epanafora ("reference"). The referring and communicating to the multitude.
Epairomenos ("raising himself"). Used instead of "stretching himself up against" by Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. But in the speech Against Aphobus he uses it in another sense: "or those roused up by gains because of want."
Epedikase ("he adjudged"). Epedikase and epedikasanto: Demosthenes in the speech Against Olympiodorus. "Epedikasen" is, as it were, "he adjudged"; "epedikasanto" is, as it were, "they persuaded the jurors to assign the estate to them." [On bringing a spear at the funeral and proclaiming at the tomb:] Demosthenes Against Euergus and Mnesibulus says these things concerning the man who died by violence. Ister, in his Collection of the Atthides, having spoken about Procris and Cephalus, writes thus: "but some say that Erechtheus was represented with a spear fixed on the tomb, sitting beside it and signifying the deed, because it was customary for the kinsmen to pursue the murderers in this fashion."
Epeskepsato. Used instead of "he charged with false testimony." It is sometimes, though rarely, also used of charging with homicide, as Antiphon in his speech Concerning the Revolution. But the active "epeskepsen," used instead of "he enjoined," Isaeus uses in the speech On Behalf of Eumathes, for the Recovery of Freedom. And "episkepto," used instead of "I speak with some adjuration and, as it were, put under oath," both Andocides in the speech On the Mysteries and Lysias in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiarchus have used.
Epibates ("marine"). Demosthenes in the speech Concerning the Supplementary Trierarchy. They so called those serving on the triremes who did not row, but were fit only for fighting. Aristophanes in the Babylonians: "well did the marine dive out, so as to carry off the . . ."
Epibaetas. Lysias in the speech Against Micinus for Homicide, if it is genuine. The "epibles" is, as Timachidas says, a beam; but as Cleitarchus the glossographer says, a certain kind of beam.
Epiboion ("supplementary offering"). Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess. Philochorus, in his second book, says thus: "if anyone sacrifices an ox to Athena, it is necessary to sacrifice a sheep also to Pandora," and the offering was called "epiboion." Likewise Staphylus too, in the first book of his work On Athens.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Epibole ("penalty"). The fine. The word is frequent among them, as also in Lysias in the speech Against Nicomachus, if the speech is genuine.
Epignomonas. Used instead of "overseers" by Lysias in the speech Concerning the Sacred Olive-Stump.
Epigrafeas ("assessors"). Those appointed to write down how much men owe to contribute to the public treasury; Lysias in the speech Concerning the Property-Tax.
Epiguion. Lysias in the speech Against Andocides for Desertion, if it is genuine. They called the stern-cables "epigyia." The poets of the old comedy too have used the word; Aristophanes in the Cargo-Ships.
Epidekaton ("the tenth in addition"). The tenth; Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras. And . . .
Epipempton eiothasi legein ("they are accustomed to say epipempton"). They are accustomed to say "epipempton" for "the fifth," as also Eupolis in the Autolycus.
Epi Delfinioi ("at the Delphinium"). It is a court so called at Athens. Here those are tried who admit they have killed but say they did so justly, as Demosthenes makes clear in his speech Against Aristocrates, and Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians.
Epidiatithesthai. Lysias in the epilogue of the speech Against Theopeithes Concerning a Guardianship. "Epidiatithesthai" is to make certain agreements, depositing a fixed sum of money with one of the intermediaries, who guarantees to each party that, if the transaction takes place, the agreed money shall by all means be paid to the other. The matter itself is called "epidiatheke," as the same orator makes clear in the speech On Behalf of Nesocles.
Epi Delioi mache ("the battle at Delium"). Lycurgus in the speech Against Lysicles. Delium is a place in Boeotia; here the Athenians, fighting, were defeated by the Boeotians, as Thucydides says in his fourth book.
Epidietes ebesai ("to have come two years past puberty"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Stephanus. Didymus says it means "if they become sixteen years old"; for "to reach puberty" is up to fourteen. But the ephebes among the Athenians are eighteen years old, and they remain among the ephebes two years, and then they are enrolled in the deme-register, as Hyperides says in the speech Against Chares Concerning a Guardianship: "but when I was enrolled, and the law restored to my mother the recovery of what had been left—the law which bids the children be masters of the heiress and of all the property, when they are two years past puberty."
Epidikos kai epikleros kai epiproikos ("subject to adjudication, heiress, dowered"). Epidikos and epikleros and epiproikos and epiklerotis: an "epikleros" is the orphan left over the whole estate, there being no brother to her (and she is the same as the "epiklerotis"); an "epiproikos" is one left over a certain part of the estate, so as to have a dowry, there being brothers to her; an "epidikos" is the disputed heiress, as to whom she must be married to. These things Isaeus shows in the speech Against Satyrus, On Behalf of an Heiress, and Dinarchus in the work entitled A Counter-Deposition Concerning the Non-Adjudicability of the Daughter of Aristophon; in which speech it is also shown that the nearest of kin used to give in marriage the destitute maidens, adding a dowry of five minas. Isaeus, in the speech Against Lysibius, called the "epikleros" an "epiklerotis."
Epi Thrasulloi ("at Thrasyllus'"). Demosthenes in the special plea Against Pantaenetus says "at Thrasyllus'." It is an Attic idiom, instead of "at the monument of Thrasyllus."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Epithetous eortas ("added festivals"). Isocrates in the Areopagiticus. They called festivals not ancestral, but otherwise voted in, "added" (epithetoi). Among them certain other things were also called "added," all those not ancestral, on which the Council of the Areopagus gave judgment, as Lysias makes clear in his speech on the indictment Against Mixidemus. Lysias, in the speech Against Thrasybulus, names certain "added letters," and he would mean those given to certain persons to carry across; for it was customary to say "he added a letter" instead of "he handed over," as Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Chrysippus, against the special plea of Phormio. Cratinus, in the Trophonius . . .
Epikekeruchenai ("to have set a price"). Demosthenes in the speech On the Embassy. Whenever a city or magistrate wished one of those not under their power to be killed, it proclaimed it would give money, so much and so much, if anyone should kill him—just as the Greeks proclaimed a price on Xerxes, that they would give a hundred talents to anyone who should bring him, alive or dead, to Athens.
Epikerukeia ("herald-overtures"). The sending of heralds about friendship and reconciliation; Demosthenes in the fifth book of the Philippics.
Epi korres ("on the cheek"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Meidias. Different men have rendered it differently, but it is better to understand "on the cheek" (epi korres) as being "on the jaw," what we call in life a "slap." Hyperides, at any rate, or Philinus, in the speech Against Dorotheus, having first said that the man who struck Hipponicus on the cheek was indicted for outrage, in what follows explains the word, as it were, saying: "then Hipponicus was merely slapped on the jaw by Autocles, but I was dragged by these hairs, and received blows of the fist."
Epikrates. Isaeus in the speech Concerning Matters Spoken in Macedonia. This is the demagogue of the Athenians surnamed "the shield-bearer," whom Demosthenes too mentions in the speech On the Embassy. There is another Epicrates whom Lycurgus mentions in the speech On the Administration, saying that he was set up in bronze on account of the law about the ephebes, and that he is said to have possessed an estate of six hundred talents. There is yet another Epicrates, the brother-in-law of Aeschines the orator, as is shown by him in his Defense on the Embassy; this man, however, had the nickname "Cyrebion," as Demosthenes says in the speech Against Aeschines.
Epilachon ("having drawn a second lot"). Aeschines Against Ctesiphon: "neither having drawn the lot nor drawn the second lot, but having bought the place by intrigue." The matter seems to be of this sort: those aspiring to be councillors or magistrates were chosen by lot, and then to each of those allotted another was allotted as substitute, so that if the first man allotted should be rejected or die, the substitute should become councillor in his place. These things are suggested in the Hyperbolus of Plato.
Epimeletes ton musterion ("superintendent of the mysteries"). Among the Athenians, the so-called king-archon; Demosthenes Against Meidias. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says thus: "the king-archon first has charge of the mysteries, together with the superintendents, whom the people elect, two from all the Athenians, one from the Eumolpidae, and one from the Heralds."
Epimeletes emporiou ("superintendent of the trading-port"). Dinarchus in the speech Against Pytheas. Aristotle: "they choose by lot ten superintendents of the trading-port, and to these it is assigned to have charge of the merchants and to compel the merchants to bring up to the city two-thirds of the grain that comes by sea into the Attic port."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Epimenia ("monthly offerings"). Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess. The "epimenia" seem to be either the things sacrificed each month, or the offerings made once for the whole month.
Epiorkesanta ("having sworn"). Lysias, Against Theomnestus, explained that "having sworn falsely" (epiorkesanta) means "having sworn (omosanta)."
Epi Palladioi ("at the Palladium"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. It is a court so called, as Aristotle too says in the Constitution of the Athenians, in which the ephetai try cases of involuntary homicide and of plotting. The court got the name "of the Palladium," and the judges the name "ephetai," from this: when Agamemnon, with the Argives, had been brought to Athens from Ilium with the Palladium, Demophon seized the Palladium and killed many of the pursuers. Agamemnon, indignant, demanded justice from the man who had seized it, and a court was set up of fifty Athenians and fifty Argives, whom they called "ephetai" because the matters of the trial had been referred (epheicthenai) to them by both parties.
Epipempton. Lysias in the speech Against Critodemus, and Plato, used instead of the simple "fifth." Aristophanes in the Banqueters: "let him not get the fifth part; let him weep."
Epiplon ("furnishings"). Isaeus in the speech Against Diocles. They call the household goods "epipla," the property that is, as it were, superficial and able to be carried about. Sophocles in the Athamas.
Epi prutaneioi ("at the Prytaneum"). This too is a homicide court; it judges if any inanimate thing, falling, kills someone—that is, if a stone or a piece of wood or iron or some such thing—and the man who threw it is unknown, but the thing itself is known and is held to have done the murder.
Episemainesthai. Used instead of "to praise" and, as we say in common speech, "to acclaim," by Isocrates in the Panathenaicus; but instead of "to set one's seal upon" by Isaeus in his defense for ejectment, Against Hagnotheus, on behalf of Calydon.
Episitia ("provisions"). The things given for food and sustenance; Lysias in the speech Against Demosthenes for Maladministration of a Guardianship. These they sometimes also called "sition."
Episkopos ("inspector"). Antiphon in his work Concerning the Tribute of the Lindians and in the speech Against Laispodias. Certain men seem to have been sent out by the Athenians to the subject cities to inspect the affairs among each. Theophrastus, at any rate, in the first book of his Politics Adapted to Occasions, says thus: "for it is far better, at least as regards the choice of name—as the Laconians, who say they send 'harmosts' to the cities, not 'inspectors' or 'guards,' as the Athenians do."
Epistates ("president"). Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes. There are two presidents established, one chosen by lot from the prytaneis, the other from the proedroi, of whom each administers what administration, Aristotle has shown in the Constitution of the Athenians. In public affairs, the man set over any matter whatever was also called "president," as Hyperides in the speech Against Demosthenes and Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon make plain.
Epistathmos ("billet-master, overseer"). Isocrates in the Panegyricus: "Hecatomnos, the overseer (epistathmos) of Caria"—which was nothing else than being master of the satrapy of Caria.
Epiteleoun ("completing"). Epiteleoun and epiteleoma: both words occur often in the speech Concerning the Priestess of Lycurgus, and "epiteleoma" seems to mean the sacrifice made after all the rest, for the sake of bringing the former sacrifices to completion. At any rate the orator himself, in the speech, says: "further, he said that these were sacrificed last of all and were the completion (epiteleomata) of the other offerings."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Epitimetas ("re-assessors"). Those first assessing anything were called "assessors" (timetai), those in the following years assessing the same things "re-assessors" (epitimetai); Lysias in the speech Against Diogenes.
Epiteichisma ("a fortified outpost"). A place fortified against certain persons, from which the fortifiers, setting out, will be able to harm those fortified against; Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. They also call the act "epiteichismos," as is in the same speech.
Epitrepein ("to entrust, to refer"). Demosthenes, in his speech Against Aphobus, book one, began thus: "if Aphobus had been willing, men of the jury, to do what is just concerning the matters in dispute between us, and to entrust them to our relatives," instead of "to choose them as arbitrators"; whence also the play of Menander, The Arbitration. Lysias, in the speech Against the Guardians of the Sons of Boeon, said "he entrusted to men," instead of "he appointed guardians."
Epitritais ("at a third in addition"). Isaeus in the speech Against Calliphon: "six hundred drachmas at a third in addition (epitritais)," instead of "at eight obols," since the eight obols are a third of the four-drachma piece.
Epichares. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. A proper name, a Sicyonian traitor.
Epicheirotonia ("election by show of hands"). The appointment of those chosen by show of hands; Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Simias against Pytheas and Lycurgus.
Epipsefizon ("putting to the vote"). Used instead of "ratifying"; Demosthenes in his speech Against Androtion. The word is frequent among the Attic writers in this meaning, as also in Xenophon in the first book of the Memorabilia.
Epogdoon ("an eighth in addition"). Demosthenes in the speech Against Polycles, Concerning the Supplementary Trierarchy. "Epogdoon" would be money lent in such a way that an eighth part of the principal is given to the lender, as three obols on the four-drachma piece.
Epobelia ("the obol-penalty"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Stephanus. The "epobelia" is a penalty, the sixth part of the assessment, which the prosecutors paid to the defendants if they did not win. It was so called because for each drachma there was an obol, which is a sixth, the drachma being reckoned at six obols. From many instances one may learn that this is so.
Eponia ("sale-tax"). It is a tax given on the purchase, and would perhaps be a fifth; Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes and in the counter-oath Against Tlepolemus.
Eponumoi ("the eponymous"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates. The "eponymous" are of two kinds: the ten, after whom the tribes are named, and the forty-two others, after whom the age-classes of the citizens are named each year, from eighteen years to sixty.
Epopteukoton ("of those initiated into the higher mysteries"). Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Phryne. Those initiated at Eleusis in the second initiation are said "to behold" (epopteuein), as is clear both from the speech of Demosthenes and from the tenth book of Philochorus.
Eranizontes ("contributing to a loan-club"). Demosthenes, in the letter concerning the sons of Lycurgus, said "having contributed (eranisas)" instead of "having asked for a loan-club"; but in the speech Concerning the Name he says: "but what if, expecting to be convicted of false testimony for the things in which he contributes (eranizei) to these men about himself, he repays in kind, rendering them equal aid to that which they once furnished, having borne false witness for him?" The "eranistes," however, is properly the one who shares in the loan-club and pays in the contribution that had to be paid each month. The word is in Lysias in the speech Against Aristocrates Concerning a Pledge of a Loan-Club, if it is genuine.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Erga neon ("works of the young"). This too Hyperides, in the speech Against Autocles, says is Hesiod's. It is a proverb, which Aristophanes the grammarian also recorded, running thus: "works are of the young, counsels of the middle-aged, prayers of the old."
Ergiske. Aeschines Against Ctesiphon. Ergiske too is of Thrace, named after Ergiscus the son of Poseidon and the nymph Aba.
Ergokles. A general of the Athenians.
Ergofilos. This man too was a general of the Athenians.
Herkeios Zeus ("Zeus of the Enclosure"). Dinarchus in the speech Against Moschion: "whether he has phratry-members and altars of Zeus of the Enclosure and of ancestral Apollo." "Herkeios" Zeus is the one whose altar is set within the enclosure (herkos) in the courtyard; for they called the enclosure "herkos." That those had a share in citizenship who had a Zeus of the Enclosure, Hyperides too has shown in the speech On Behalf of a Made Citizen, if it is genuine, and Demetrius in his work On the Legislation at Athens.
Herma ("reef"). The submerged rock; Antiphon in his Defense Against the Information of Callias. The word is also in Anacreon and in the Gerytades of Aristophanes.
Hermai ("the Herms"). Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon, and Hyperides in the speech Concerning the Gifts of Eubulus. Menecles or Callicrates, in the work On Athens, writes thus: "from the Painted Stoa and the Royal Stoa are the so-called Herms; for, because many were set up both by private men and by magistrates, it came about that they received this name." On one of them is inscribed in ancient letters: "In return for their benefaction the Achaeans bound Agamemnon." That a certain stoa was also called the Stoa of the Herms, Antiphon too has shown in the speech Against Nicocles. That certain Herms were also called "Hipparchian," after Hipparchus the son of Peisistratus, has been said both in the old comedy and in Plato in the Hipparchus.
Hermos. It is a deme of Attica, of the tribe Acamantis, as Diodorus says in his work On the Demes. But Dionysius the son of Tryphon, in his work On Names, says that the name of the deme, "Hermos," is seemingly neuter, like "herkos." Zopyrus, in his work On Rivers, says there is a "Hermos" in Attica and a deme of the same name as it.
Hermes ho pros tei pulidi ("the Hermes by the little gate"). Demosthenes in the speech Against Euergus and Mnesibulus. Philochorus, in the fifth book of his Atthis, says that the nine archons set up for the tribes a Hermes by the gateway, the Attic one.
Hermias. A proper name, the eunuch who had been thrice sold. He stood on intimate terms with Aristotle, and gave his adopted daughter to the philosopher.
Eroiadai. The Eroiadae are a deme of the tribe Hippothontis, as Diodorus says.
Eruthraioi. Demosthenes in the eighth Philippic. Erythrae is a city in Ionia, one of those founded by Neleus the son of Codrus, as Hellanicus says in his Atthis.
Erchiathen ("from Erchia"). Dinarchus Against Stephanus. Erchia is a deme of the tribe Aegeis, as Diodorus says.
Espathato. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aeschines. Didymus says it is used instead of "was wasted," from the "spathe"; and "spathe" is a sword. Perhaps, however, the metaphor is from weavers; for they use a "spathe" (a weaving-blade). And Aristophanes in the Clouds: "wife, you weave too lavishly (spathas)."
Estiator ("host, feast-giver"). The man who sets a table before certain people; Demosthenes in the speech Against Boeotus. They feasted the tribes, some willingly, some by lot, as the same orator makes clear in the speech Against Meidias.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Eschara ("hearth"). Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess. Ammonius, in his work On Altars, says that the "eschara" is called the hearth that has no height, but is set low on the ground and hollow; from which the physicians too call the hollow ulcers in bodies "escharai."
Eschatia ("the outlying land"). Demosthenes in the speech Against Phaenippus. They called the lands at the borders of the plots "eschatiai," the ones bordered by either a mountain or the sea.
Hetaireia ("companionship"). In a special sense Andocides applied the word to prostitution (hetairesis) in his Defense on the Mysteries.
Eteoboutadai. Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess. A clan among the Athenians, as it were "those truly from Butes"; for "eteon" means "true." From these was established the priestess of Athena Polias, as Draco says in his work On Clans.
Heterofthalmos ("the one-eyed man"). The one who made laws among the Locrians; Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates.
Euagoras. A proper name, for whom the encomium of Isocrates is composed.
Euaion. Demosthenes Against Meidias. A proper name.
Euandria ("the contest of manhood"). Dinarchus in the speech Against Agasikles. At the Panathenaea a contest of manhood (euandria) was held. Andocides makes this clear in the speech Against Alcibiades, and Philochorus.
Euboulos. There is a speech of Hyperides Concerning the Gifts of Eubulus, and Demosthenes mentions him in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. That he was a most distinguished demagogue, careful and industrious, and that, providing much money for the Athenians, he distributed it, on which account it came about that the city, under his administration, became most unmanly and most slothful—Theopompus says in the tenth book of the Philippics. There is another, the comic poet, whom Hyperides mentions in the speech Against Archestratides.
Eudikos. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. This man was one of those established by Philip as masters of all Thessaly.
Euenos. Hyperides in the speech Against Autocles. They record two Euenoi, elegiac poets of the same name, as Eratosthenes does in his work On Chronologies, saying that both were Parians; but he says that only the younger is well known. Plato too mentions one of them.
Eueniotata ("most tractably"). Antiphon in his work On Concord. "Euenios" is the gentle and moderate and not turbulent man; the metaphor is from horses. The word is also in Plato in the ninth book of the Laws.
Euthias. Hyperides On Behalf of Phryne. Euthias was among those reputed for malicious prosecution. Hermippus says that Anaximenes composed for him the speech Against Phryne.
Euthunoi ("examiners"). Lysias in the speech Against Nicides, if it is genuine. "Euthynoi" is the name of a magistracy among the Athenians. They were ten men in number, before whom those who had served on embassies or held office or administered any public matter rendered their accounts (euthynai). Aristotle has discoursed about them in the Constitution of the Athenians.
Euthuoron ("straight ahead"). The going in a straight line; Antiphon in the speech Against Nicocles. The word is also in Xenophon in the second book of the Anabasis.
Eumenides. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. Aeschylus, in the Eumenides, having told of the trial of Orestes, says that Athena, having soothed the Erinyes so that they were not harsh toward Orestes, named them "Eumenides" (Kindly Ones). They are Alecto, Megaera, and Tisiphone.
Euneidai. Lysias in the speech Against Telamon, if it is genuine. There is a clan among the Athenians so named, the Euneidae; they were lyre-players who furnished their service for the sacred rites.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Euxitheos. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon, says that by this man the Eleans were betrayed.
Euoi saboi ("euoi saboi"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. "Euoi" is a Bacchic exclamation. Arignote says that some said "euoi" instead of "well to you" (eu soi), praising the invention of the mirror.
Euofthalmos ("with fair appearance"). Used instead of "seemly" by Antiphon in his work On Peacocks.
Eurubaton ("Eurybatus"). Aeschines Against Ctesiphon. Ephorus, in his eighth book, says that Eurybatus, a man of Ephesus, having taken money from Croesus to gather an army for the war against the Persians, then turned traitor and handed over the money given him to Cyrus, and that from this base men are called "Eurybatoi."
Eurumedon. Lycurgus in the speech Against Leocrates. Eurymedon is a river of Pamphylia, where Cimon, general of the Athenians, defeated the Persians both by land and by sea, as Thucydides says in his first book.
Eurusakeion. Hyperides in the speech Against Aristogiton. It is a precinct of Eurysaces the son of Ajax at Athens, so named, in Melite.
Eusumbolos ("easy to deal with"). Used instead of "easily and well dealing," that is, "good at dealing," by Antiphon in the Political speech.
Eufraios. Demosthenes in the ninth Philippic. This man was an Oreite by birth, and he had a share in the school of Plato.
Euonumeis. Lysias in the speech Against Philocrates. It is a deme of the tribe Erechtheis, as Diodorus says.
Efesis ("appeal"). The transfer from one court to another; the same is also called "ekkletos." There is a speech of Demosthenes entitled An Appeal Against Eubulides, and in the speech the word "appeal" and the verb "to appeal" occur often.
Efektos tokos ("interest at a sixth"). Interest at the sixth part of the principal; Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Chrysippus.
Efetai ("the ephetai"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. Those who judged the cases of bloodshed at the Palladium and at the Prytaneum and at the Delphinium and at Phreatto were called "ephetai."
Ef ieron ("to the shrine"). Demosthenes in the speech Concerning the Supplementary Trierarchy. There is a shrine of the twelve gods on the Bosporus, as Timosthenes says in his work On Harbors.
Eforia. The proclamation made at the boundaries, as Demosthenes teaches in his speech Against Aristocrates, and Theophrastus in the third book of his Laws.
Eformein ("to lie at anchor against"). Used instead of "to lie in wait"; for the lying off against certain persons, watching for an opportunity of attack, was so called; Demosthenes in the Philippics.
Echinos. It is a vessel into which the documents for the suits were put; Demosthenes in the speech Against Timotheus. Aristotle mentions this vessel too in the Constitution of the Athenians, and Aristophanes in the Danaids. There was also a city, Echinus, which Demosthenes mentions in the eighth Philippic. There is also a certain creature, both of land and of the sea, a shellfish.
Heolokrasia ("the dregs of stale wine"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "this man is the cause, having poured over me, as it were, a kind of dregs of his own wickedness." Didymus says: "the matters which he stirred up yesterday and the day before, today he pours over me and says that I did them."
6. Zeira. Zeira, or "seira": as some say, it was a garment which they put on over their tunics like a cloak; Lysias in the speech Against Philip, if it is genuine. And Xenophon, in the seventh book of the Anabasis, speaking of the Thracians, says: "they wore long robes (zeirai) reaching to their feet upon their horses, and not cloaks."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Zeuxis. Isocrates, On the Exchange of Property. The best of the painters of that time.
Zelotupoun ("to be jealous"). Aeschines, in the speech Against Ctesiphon, used instead of "to hate"; for "to envy" (zeloun) is "to count blessed," while "to be jealous" (zelotupein) is "to have come into enmity."
Zetetes ("investigator"). A magistracy at Athens established as occasion required, whenever it was necessary to seek out those committing some public wrong; Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates, and Andocides in the speech On the Information. This orator too once became an investigator, as Lysias and Isocrates say, and Plato the comic poet in the Ambassadors.
7. Hegemonia dikasteriou ("presidency of a court"). Aeschines Against Ctesiphon. Different suits were brought before different magistrates, and the magistrates introduced the suits brought to them into court, each according to its own law, presiding and taking the lead: thus, before the archon, the suits concerning orphans and heiresses; before the king-archon, those of impiety; before the polemarch, those of desertion and of being without a patron; before the thesmothetai, those of alien status and of bribery-for-citizenship and of malicious prosecution and of bribes and of false registration and of outrage and of adultery and of plotting and others.
Hegemon summorias ("leader of a symmory"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. The man who excelled in wealth, and on that account was charged with leading the rest, was called the "leader of the symmory," as Hyperides suggests in his speech Against Polyeuctus.
Hegemon. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. He was one of those who favored the Macedonians and were charged with taking bribes.
Hegesippos. Demosthenes in a Philippic. This is the one surnamed Crobylus, to whom some think the seventh Philippic ascribed to Demosthenes belongs.
Heduleion. Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aeschines. The Hedyleion is a mountain in Boeotia, as Theopompus says in his twenty-fifth book. "Or having brought down on the road": instead of "having taken him while lying in ambush," that is, "having struck him down in some ambush"; Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates.
Eetioneia. Antiphon, in his speech Concerning the Revolution. So was named the other headland of the Piraeus, after Eetion who acquired the land, as Philochorus says in his Counter-Plea against Demon. Thucydides too mentions the Eetioneia in his eighth book.
Ekroteriasmenoi ("mutilated"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "having each mutilated their own native lands," instead of "having ravaged them"; for those who maltreat people are accustomed to cut off their extremities, as Sophocles too in the Polyxena. Here, however, "mutilated" stands in place of the active "having mutilated."
Heliaia. Heliaia and heliasis: the heliaia is the greatest court at Athens, in which the public matters were judged, with a thousand or fifteen hundred jurors gathering. The thousand came together from two courts, the fifteen hundred from three. "To sit in the heliaia" and "heliasis" mean to give judgment in the heliaia. Lysias, in the speech Against Glaucon, often names the heliaia, but in the speech Against Philonides, if it is genuine, he used "to sit in the heliaia."
Helikia tes poleos ("the prime of the city"). Used instead of "those in their prime, the young men"; Lycurgus Against Aristogiton, and Demosthenes in the Philippics.
Hemiekton ("half-sixth measure"). Hemiekton and hemimedimnon: Dinarchus in the information Against Callisthenes. The medimnos containing forty-eight choinikes, the measure holding twenty-four choinikes is a half-medimnon; the half-sixth (hemiekton) is the measure holding four choinikes, the half of the sixth-part, which is eight choinikes.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Hemioliasmos ("a reckoning by one-and-a-half"). Antiphon, in the Political speech: "of doubling and of reckoning by one-and-a-half," instead of "to give the one-and-a-half measure in the calculations." The number "hemiolios" is one that contains another whole and the half of it, as three to two. At any rate Xenophon, in the Anabasis, says that he made the pay of the soldiers one-and-a-half, three half-darics instead of a daric.
Epeiron ("the mainland"). It is customary for Isocrates to call the land under the king of the Persians by this name, as in both the To Philip and the Archidamus.
Herakleia. Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aeschines. There being many Heracleia throughout Attica, Demosthenes would now mean either those at Marathon or those at Cynosarges; for these especially the Athenians held in honor.
Heraion teichos ("the wall of Hera"). Demosthenes in the Philippics. It is a place in Thrace so called, settled by the Samians, as Dionysius says in the fifth book of his Foundations.
Eria ("tombs"). Lycurgus, in the speech Against Autolycus. The "eria" are the tombs, as the orator himself makes clear. Some say that more generally all tombs are so called, but in a special sense those whose monuments are not raised on high, but where the bodies are laid in the earth; and that the name comes from "era" (the earth).
Esmen ("we knew"). Used instead of "we knew" (edeimen). Antiphon, in his Defense Against the Information of Callias: "we, then, neither knew (esmen) how great a fleet was needed."
Eitemenen ("borrowed"). Used instead of "having been lent" by Demosthenes in the speech Against Euergus, if it is genuine. For that they used "to ask" (aiteisthai) for "to borrow," Menander shows: "for not asking for fire, nor begging a dish."
Hefaistia. Hyperides, in the speech On Behalf of Academus. That there were two cities of Lemnos, Myrina and Hephaestia, Dionysius of Chalcis too makes clear in the third book of his Foundations.
Eion. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. Eion is a city of Thrace, a colony of the Mendaeans, as Thucydides says. But Theopompus, in his fourth book, says that the Athenians, having driven the Amphipolitans out of Eion, razed the place.
8. Thargelia. Hyperides, in the speech Against Polyeuctus. The Thargelia is a festival, held in the month Thargelion, which is sacred to Apollo.
Themenos ta opla ("having put on his arms"). Used instead of "having girded on and armed himself" by Demosthenes in his speech Against Meidias. And Homer: "and on his mighty head he set the helmet." And Aeschines, in the speech Against Timarchus, says: "fellow, for the city for which you do not put on your arms (tithesai)."
Themisteuein ("to deliver oracles"). Used instead of "to give oracular responses" by Lysias in the speech On the Miscarriage, if it is genuine. That the word came from Themis once having held the oracle before Apollo, Aeschylus says at the beginning of the Eumenides.
Themison. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. A proper name. This man became a tyrant.
Theogeiton. Demosthenes in the same speech. Some named this man Theogenes, as Dinarchus too does in the speech Against Demosthenes.
Theognis. Lysias in the speech Against Eratosthenes. This man was one of the Thirty tyrants at Athens, as others say, and Xenophon in the second book of the Hellenica. Of the poet Theognis, Isocrates makes mention in his admonitions To Nicocles; this man was a Megarian, from the Megara near Attica; for the poet himself says . . . Plato, in the first book of the Laws, not having attended to this, asserted that he was a citizen of the Megarians in Sicily. Not a few followed Plato in this.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Theoinion. Lycurgus in the adjudication of the Croconidae against the Coeronidae. The Dionysia held in the demes were called Theoinia, in which the clansmen offered sacrifice; for they called Dionysus "Theoinos," as Aeschylus shows, and Ister in the first book of his Collections.
Theokrines. Demosthenes, in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon, reviling Aeschines, says "a tragic Theocrines." He means to call him a malicious prosecutor, since Theocrines was such a man, as is clear from the speech Against Theocrines, whether this speech is by Demosthenes or by Dinarchus. Since the man had once been a tragic actor and afterward a malicious prosecutor, he fittingly named him "a tragic Theocrines."
Therapnai. Isocrates in the Helen. There is a place in Lacedaemon called Therapnae, which Alcman too mentions in his first book.
Therman. Aeschines in his Defense on the Embassy. This is a Thracian town, as Theopompus too says in his twenty-second book.
Thermopulai. Isocrates in the Panegyricus. Some call this town "Pylae"; but Phileas, in his Description of the Earth, says it was called Thermopylae because there Athena made warm baths (therma loutra) for Heracles.
Thersandros. Aeschines Against Timarchus. That this man was a violent lover of boys, Aristogiton too makes clear in the speech Against Timarchus.
Thesthai ("to take as security, to enact"). Used instead of "to take as a pledge" by Hyperides in the speech Against Hygiaenon, but instead of "to receive and ratify a law" by Demosthenes; for in the case of laws it is said that "the lawgiver laid down (etheke), and the people enacted (etheto)"; Demosthenes in the speech On the Immunities.
