But in the speech Against Stephanus he says "having enacted private laws for himself," perhaps instead of "having laid down."
Thesmos ("ordinance"). Of old each single one of the laws was called a "thesmos," and Demosthenes too has so called the whole framework of the constitution in his speech Against Aristocrates.
Thesmothetai. Demosthenes in his speech Against Androtion. There is a magistracy at Athens, that of the thesmothetai, six in number; they are among the so-called nine archons. They are so called because they had charge of the laws; for the laws were called "thesmoi," as we said before. That these men revised the laws each year, Aeschines has said in the speech Against Ctesiphon, and Theophrastus in the third book of his Laws. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, goes through all that they do.
Thetes ("one who has given security"). Perhaps they call "thetes" the man who has given a pledge, and not, as Didymus says, the man who has adopted a son; for they called the adopted "thetoi," he says.
Thettalos. Lysias Against Nicides. One of the sons of Cimon was called Thettalus, as Heliodorus says in his work On the Acropolis.
Theudosian. Demosthenes in his speech On the Immunities. It is a place lying near the Scythians, which Satyrus died while besieging.
Theorika ("festival-funds"). Demosthenes in a Philippic. The "theorika" were certain public moneys, gathered from the revenues of the city; these were formerly kept for the needs of war and called "military funds," but afterward were laid out both on public works and on distributions, of which Agyrrhius the demagogue was the first to begin. Philochorus, in the third book of his Atthis, says: "the theorikon was first reckoned at a drachma for the show, whence it took its name," and what follows. But Philinus, in his speech against the statues of Sophocles and Euripides, speaking of Eubulus, says: "it was called theorikon because, the Dionysia being at hand, Eubulus distributed money for the sacrifice, so that all might keep the festival and no citizen be left out of the spectacle through want of private means." At different times, however, different sums were fixed for the spectacles and the sacrifices and festivals, as is clear from the first of the Philippics of Demosthenes. That it was not permitted to those abroad to take the theorikon, Hyperides has shown in his speech Against Archestratides. There was also a magistracy over the theorikon, as Aeschines shows in the speech Against Ctesiphon. "Theoroi," moreover, are not only the spectators, but also those sent to the gods; and in general they so named those who guard or have care of divine matters; for they called concern "ore." "For little is the concern (ore) of quarrels and of assemblies."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Theoris. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristogiton, if it is genuine. Theoris was a seeress, and being judged for impiety she was put to death, as Philochorus too writes in his sixth book.
Themakeus. Andocides in the speech On the Mysteries. Themakos is a deme of the tribe Erechtheis, as Diodorus the geographer says in his work On the Demes.
Theramenes. Lysias in the speech Against Eratosthenes. He was put to death, Critias having accused him, under the Thirty.
Theseion. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is a precinct dedicated to Theseus.
Thetes ("thetes, the laboring class"). Thetes and thetikon: Antiphon, in the speech Against Philinus, says "to make all the thetes hoplites," and Demosthenes, in the speech Concerning the Estate of Hagnias, "of the heiresses, those who pay the thetic rate." The constitution being divided among the Athenians into four classes, the poorest were called "thetes" and were said "to pay the thetic rate." These men shared in no office, as Aristotle too shows in the Constitution of the Athenians. That they did not serve in the army, Aristophanes too has said in the Banqueters. Demosthenes, in the passage before us, called the poor girl an "heiress," whom the Attic writers name a "thessa." It was incumbent on the nearest of kin either to take the "thessai" in marriage or to give five minas, as Posidippus the comic poet too says somewhere.
Thiasos ("religious guild"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Aeschines. A "thiasos" is the multitude gathered for the celebration and honor of the gods; Xenophon in the second book of the Memorabilia. But Ion, in the Omphale, applied the word in general to every gathering. The "thiasotai" were those who shared in the guilds; Isaeus in the speech Concerning the Estate of Astyphilus.
Thibron. Isocrates in the Panegyricus. This man was a Lacedaemonian sent into Asia as harmost after the Peloponnesian War.
Tholos ("the Rotunda"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Aeschines. The place where the prytaneis dined was so called among the Athenians. Ammonius, at any rate, in the fourth book of his work On Altars, writes thus: "the place where the prytaneis are entertained is called the Tholos, but by some the 'Shade,' because it was built round, resembling a sunshade (tholia)."
Thorai. A deme of the tribe Antiochis, as Diodorus says.
Thorikos. Isaeus in the speech Against Posidippus. It is a deme of the tribe Acamantis, as the same Diodorus says in his work On the Demes.
Thripedeston ("worm-eaten"). Hyperides, in the speech Against Demades, called Greece "worm-eaten," instead of "ruined," from wood eaten away by woodworms (thripes).
Thronion. Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. Thronion is a city of Locris, as Theopompus says in his . . .
Thumaitadai. A deme of the tribe Hippothontis, named after the hero Thymaetes, as Diodorus says.
Thurgonidai. Isaeus in the speech Against Nicocles. Nicander of Thyateira, in his work On the Demes, says that the Aphidnaeans, the Perridae, the Titacidae, and the Thyrgonidae were transferred from the tribe Aeantis. Demetrius of Scepsis too, in the second book of his Order, says that the deme belongs to the tribe Ptolemais.
Thustion. Aeschines Against Ctesiphon. It is a city of Aetolia, as Didymus says, citing as witness the first book of the Aetolica of Nicander. We, however, in the Atticianus copies found it written with a tau, "Thytion."
9. Idian ("private"). Used instead of "private" by Demosthenes in his speech Against Conon. They used "idion" and "idiotikon" alike, as the same orator does in the speech Against Zenothemis.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Idrieus. Isocrates, in the speech To Philip. This man was a dynast in Caria, son of Hecatomnos, brother of Mausolus and Artemisia.
Hierax. Demosthenes in the first book of the Philippics. That Hierax was one of the envoys sent by the Amphipolitans to Athens, when they wished to hand over both their city and their territory to the Athenians, Theopompus has said in the third book of the Philippics.
Hiera odos ("the Sacred Way"). Isaeus, in his Defense Against Diophanes. The Sacred Way is the one by which the initiates go from the city to Eleusis. A whole book has been written by Polemon concerning the Sacred Way. Cratinus too mentions it in the Runaway Women.
Hiera trieres ("the sacred trireme"). Demosthenes in the fourth book of the Philippics: "and he went off, taking the sacred trireme from the country." He would mean the Paralus, as may be gathered both from Philochorus and likewise from the sixth book of Androtion.
Hieromenia ("sacred month"). Demosthenes Against Timocrates. The festival-days are called "hieromeniai."
Hieromnemones ("sacred recorders"). Demosthenes On Behalf of Ctesiphon. Those sent to the council of the Amphictyons from each of the cities sharing in the council are so called, as Theopompus makes clear in his thirtieth book.
Hierofantes ("hierophant"). Hyperides says somewhere: "but I have neither a torchbearer's daughter nor a hierophant's." Dinarchus, in the adjudication of the Croconidae, says that the first hierophant was so named because he revealed (apophenanta) the sacred things when returning from war. Concerning the clan of the hierophants, Hellanicus has shown in the second book of his Atthis.
Hieronumos. Lysias in the speech Against Hippotherses. Of Hieronymus who served as general of the Athenians, others make mention, and Ephorus both in his eighteenth and in his nineteenth book. There is another Hieronymus, a Megalopolitan, whom Demosthenes mentions in the speech Against Aeschines. That this man was especially among those who favored the Macedonians, Theopompus too has said in his fifty-first book.
Ithufalloi. Hyperides, in the speech Against Archestratides: "those who dance the ithyphalloi in the orchestra." Certain poems were so called, those sung at the phallus, as Lynceus says in his Letters. But Demosthenes, in the speech Against Conon, applied it to certain men on whom the name had been laid in jest. Properly, "ithyphallus" meant the erect member, as Cratinus uses it in the Archilochi.
Ikarieus. Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras. It is a deme of the tribe Aegeis, as Diodorus says.
Hiketeria ("suppliant-branch"). Aeschines in his Defense. The "hiketeria" is an olive branch wreathed with a fillet.
Ionios ("Ionian"). Lysias in the Olympiacus. The ancients sometimes named the so-called Adriatic thus. Epidamnus is a city on the right as one sails into the Ionian Gulf; Thucydides in his first book.
Ipnos ("kitchen"). Lycurgus in the speech Against Lycophron, book one. A part of the house is so called, what is called among us the "kitchen"; at any rate there is a play of Pherecrates, Ipnos, or the All-Night Festival, in which this is shown, that it is a part of the house. Properly, the "ipnos" is the oven, whence they also call certain men "oven-moulders."
Hipparchos. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. This man was a tyrant of Eretria. There is another Hipparchus about whom Lycurgus speaks in the speech Against Lycophron, "Hipparchus the son of Peisistratus." There is yet another Hipparchus, the son of Charmus, as Lycurgus says in the speech Against Leocrates; about him Androtion, in his second book, says that he was a kinsman of Peisistratus the tyrant and was the first to be ostracized, the law about ostracism being then first laid down, on account of the suspicion against the followers of Peisistratus, that, being a demagogue and a general, he might make himself tyrant. There is another Hipparchus, an actor, whom Demosthenes mentions in the speech Against Neaera, if it is genuine. Among the Athenians, moreover, the "hipparch" is also the commander of the cavalry; there were two of these, as Demosthenes says in the fourth book of the Philippics, and Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Hippas ("knight's rate"). Isaeus, in the speech Concerning the Estate of Apollodorus: "he registered a small assessment, as paying at the knight's rate." Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says that Solon divided the whole multitude of the Athenians into four classes: the five-hundred-bushel men, the knights (hippeis), the yoke-men, and the thetes. The "hippades," then, belong to the knights.
Hippia Athena ("Athena of the Horse"). Isaeus, in the speech Against Calydon. Mnaseas, in the first book of his Europe, says that Athena of the Horse is the daughter of Poseidon and of Coryphe daughter of Oceanus, and that, having first constructed a chariot, she was for this reason called "of the horse."
Hippodameia. Demosthenes, in the speech Against Timotheus, says there is a marketplace in the Piraeus called Hippodameia, after Hippodamus of Miletus, the architect who built the Piraeus for the Athenians.
Isa bainon Puthoklei ("walking in step with Pythocles"). Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aeschines, used instead of "always being with him and not standing apart even a little." And in the speech Against Stephanus, book one, he says "he walked in step (isa bainon) with Aristolochus the banker." Menander: "an expensive courtesan walking in step beside him."
Isai psefoi ("equal votes"). Aeschines Against Ctesiphon: "another private man who sailed to Rhodes, because he had borne his fear unmanfully, was once recently impeached, and the votes for him came out equal; but if one vote had fallen over, he would have been banished and put to death."
Isaios. This man is one of the ten orators, a pupil of Isocrates, the teacher of Demosthenes, an Athenian by birth, as Hermippus says in the second book of his work On the Pupils of Isocrates. But Demetrius, in his work On Poets of the Same Name, says he was a Chalcidian.
Ismenias. Lysias in the speech Against Thrasybulus, if it is genuine. He was one of the distinguished polemarchs among the Thebans.
Isolaites. Hyperides, in the speech On Behalf of Phryne. A certain foreign deity, to whom common women, not at all respectable, performed rites.
Isoteles ("paying equal taxes"). Isoteles and isoteleia: Isaeus often, in the speech Against Elpagoras. A certain honor given to those metics who appeared worthy, by which they also obtained release from the alien-tax, as Lysias says in the speech Against Sostratus for Outrage, if it is genuine. That the "isoteleis" had release also from the other obligations of the metics, Theophrastus has said in the eleventh book of his Laws; and he says that in some places the Athenians voted "isoteleia" to whole cities, as to the Olynthians and Thebans. One may also learn from the speech of Isaeus mentioned above how much the "isoteles" paid.
Ischandros. Demosthenes Against Aeschines. Ischandros is a tragic actor. Aeschines the orator, acting along with him, is thought to have fallen down in Collytus, as Demochares says in his Dialogues.
Itelios. Lysias in the speech Against Nicides. Itea is a deme of the tribe Acamantis, from which the demesman is Iteaeus, as Diodorus says.
Ion. Isocrates, in the speech On the Exchange of Property. The orator would now be mentioning Ion the tragic poet, who was a Chian by birth, son of Orthomenes, surnamed son of Xuthus. He wrote many lyric poems and tragedies, and a philosophical treatise entitled the Triagmus, which Callimachus says is disputed as being by Epigenes; in some copies it is entitled in the plural, Triagmoi, as Demetrius of Scepsis and Apollonides of Nicaea say. They record in it these words: "This is the beginning of my discourse: all things are three, and nothing more nor less than these three. Of each one of these three the excellence is a triad: understanding and power and fortune."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
10. Kabule. Demosthenes in the eighth book of the Philippics. It is a place of Thrace, as Theopompus says in his forty-seventh book and Anaximenes in the eighth book of the Philippics. The latter says it is situated by the river Taxus in the middle of Thrace.
Kadiskos ("voting-urn"). Isaeus in the speech Concerning the Estate of Hagnias. They so called a certain vessel into which the jurors cast their votes. Phrynichus in the Muses: "Look, take the vote. Here is your urn (kadiskos): this one acquits, that one over there condemns."
Kadmeia. Isocrates in the Panegyricus. The other orators too often mention the Cadmeia; the citadel of the Thebans is so called, as is agreed among nearly all the historians.
Katharsion ("purificatory offering"). Aeschines Against Timarchus. It was a custom at Athens to purify the assembly and the theaters and, in general, the gatherings of the people with very small piglets, which they called "katharsia." This was done by those called "peristiarchoi," who were so named either from going around (peristeichein) or from the hearth (hestia).
Kathelon ("having struck down"). Demosthenes, in his speech Against Aristocrates, says "or having struck down on the road," instead of "having killed or slain." Others too used the word thus, as Stesichorus in the Sack of Troy and Sophocles in the Eumelus.
Kathekonta ("things befalling, duties"). Demosthenes, in the tenth book of the Philippics, says "whoever did not think fit to do the things befalling upon himself," instead of "the things that come upon him."
Kathetos ("the lowered lamb"). The lamb let down into the sea; Lysias in the speech Against Telamon. Concerning the "kathetos" Meliton has discoursed in the first book of his work On the Clans at Athens.
Kai ("and"). "For even the fact that none of the fighting men, without the magistrates' . . ."
Gnomes apodemein ("resolve, to go abroad"). When Isocrates says this in the Busiris about the Lacedaemonians, one must say that those who wrote the constitutions of the Lacedaemonians have said the like; for Aristotle says that it was not permitted to the Lacedaemonians to go abroad, lest they grow accustomed to be friends of other laws than their own. But while Isocrates says that only the fighting men were prevented from going abroad, the followers of Aristotle say that all the Lacedaemonians were.
Kainos ("in a new way"). Isocrates in the Panegyricus, that is, "as befits more recent matters." Ephorus explained it in a certain way in his first book.
Kakotechnion ("of malicious contrivance"). The name of a suit, which those who had convicted someone of false testimony brought against the man who produced him; Demosthenes in the speech Against Timotheus for Repayment, if it is genuine, and in the speech Against Euergus and Mnesibulus.
Kakos eidotes ("knowing ill"). Used instead of "being ignorant" by Isocrates in the speech On the Peace.
Kakoseos ("of maltreatment"). The name of a suit, granted to heiresses against those who have married them, to children against their parents, and to those who proceed against guardians on behalf of orphans; Demosthenes Against Timocrates, and Lysias both in the speech Concerning the Estate of Hegesander and in the speech On Behalf of . . . , and Hyperides Concerning the Estate of Pyrrandrus. That it was permitted to anyone who wished to indict for the maltreatment of parents and to come to the aid of heiresses, is made clear both in the speech of Hyperides mentioned above and in the speech of Lysias Against Philonides for Violence, if it is genuine. It was also without water.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Kalaureia. Demosthenes in his letter concerning his own return. It is an island near Troezen, as Hecataeus said in his Description of the Earth. Calauria was formerly called Eirene, as Anticleides says.
Kaneforoi ("basket-bearers"). Lycurgus in the speech Against Lycophron. Concerning the basket-bearers, Philochorus, in the second book of his Atthis, says that in the reign of Erichthonius the maidens of rank were first appointed to carry the baskets for the goddess, on which lay the implements for the sacrifice, both at the Panathenaea and in the other processions.
Karkinos ("crab"). Lysias, in the Defense Concerning the Dog, if it is genuine: "for the bitches kept coming in and damaging my crab." And when the grain takes root in the earth, they say it has "crabbed"; Pherecrates in the Deserters: "whenever you have leisure, sprinkle it, that the crops may crab together." "Karkinos" is also the name of a certain ailment occurring in bodies, which they now call "carcinoma." It is also a proper name, which Isocrates mentions in the Trapeziticus; this would be the Athenian general sent to sail around the Peloponnese. Concerning the tragic poet, the son of Xenocles, Lysias speaks in the speech Against Mnesimachus: "and Carcinus the poet agrees with these, having said, 'It was not wine that drove them out of their senses; for no occasion stirs up wits rightly fixed by nature . . . to err.'"
Karpou dike ("suit for produce"). Lysias in the speech Against Demosthenes for Maladministration of a Guardianship: "for if you make any claim against this young man and he holds anything of yours, bring suit against him according to the laws—if you dispute a plot of land, a suit for produce; if a house, a suit for rent—just as he now sues you for maladministration of a guardianship."
Karuanda. Dinarchus in his speech Against Polyeuctus. It is a city of Caria.
Katabole ("an instalment, an onset"). Demosthenes in the ninth Philippic: "like a period or onset (katabole) of a fever." In recurrent diseases a certain "onset" is so called, because it comes on at a fixed time, just as the members of a loan-club make their instalments (katabolai) of money.
Katadedesthai. Used instead of "to be bewitched and bound with drugs" by Dinarchus in the information Against Pytheas.
Kata demous dikastas ("the deme-judges"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates. Concerning the deme-judges—that formerly they were thirty and went around the demes giving judgment, then became forty—Aristotle has spoken in the Constitution of the Athenians.
Katadikasamenos. Used instead of "having won and caused someone to be condemned" by Isaeus in the speech Against Diocles for Outrage.
Katagein ta ploia ("to bring the ships to land"). Demosthenes in the eighth Philippic. "To bring the ships to land" is used instead of "to use force and do harm, and not to allow those sailing to sail where they wish, but to bring them to land for the pirates at their own places," as Lycurgus too makes clear in the speech Against Leocrates.
Katastasis ("establishment-money"). Lysias: "and that the phylarchs vote to register those who served in the cavalry, that you may exact the establishment-money from them." It seems to be money which the cavalrymen appointed received from the public treasury on their appointment, as the orator himself suggests in what follows. Eupolis too indicates this in the Friends: "you did not act wisely, old man, in taking this establishment-money suddenly before you had even learned horsemanship." It is stated still more clearly in the Syrphax of Plato. The money was repaid by those who had served in the cavalry, when others were established in their place; and the phylarchs demanded it.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Kata ten agoran apseudein ("to tell no falsehood in the marketplace"). Hyperides, in the speech Against Athenogenes, book one: "the law bids one tell no falsehood in the marketplace." The law seems to concern the goods for sale; at any rate Theophrastus, in his work On Laws, says that the market-officers must attend to these two things, the good order in the marketplace and the telling of no falsehood, not only by the sellers but also by the buyers.
Katatome ("the cutting"). Hyperides in the speech Against Demosthenes: "and sitting below, under the cutting (katatome)." Philochorus, in his sixth book, writes thus: "Aeschraeus of Anagyrous dedicated the tripod above the theater, overlaying it with silver, having won as choregus for boys the year before, and inscribed it on the cutting of the rock."
Katapaex ("astonished"). One continually struck; Lysias in the speech Against Aeschines the Socratic, and in the speech Against Andocides for Impiety, if the speech is genuine. Theopompus in the Tisamenus: "but Eileithyia has pardon, being struck astonished (kataplex) at her craft by the women."
Katachusmata ("things poured down"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Stephanus, book one. That the masters poured sweetmeats over the newly-bought slaves, Aristophanes makes clear in the Plutus; and that they did so also for those returning from a sacred mission . . . They poured them also over bridegrooms, as Theopompus shows in the Hedychares.
Katacheirotonia ("condemnation by show of hands"). It was a custom at Athens to lay denunciations against the magistrates and against the malicious prosecutors before the people; and if someone was condemned by show of hands, he was brought into court. The word occurs often both in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Meidias, and in Hyperides, in the speech On Behalf of Chaerephilus Concerning the Salt-Fish. Theophrastus too has treated of condemnation by show of hands in the fourth book of his Laws.
Katapseudomarturesamenos. Used instead of "having produced those who would bear false witness" by Demosthenes in his speech Against Stephanus.
Kateleusan. Used instead of "they cast down with stones" by Hyperides in the speech Against Autocles.
Katoikodomesen. Used instead of "he shut up in a chamber and killed" by Isaeus, often, in the speech Against Diocles.
Kebrena. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. Cebren is a city of the Troad, a colony of the Cymaeans, as Ephorus says in his first book.
Kegchreon ("the millet-house"). Demosthenes in the special plea Against Pantaenetus: "and then he persuaded my slaves to sit down in the millet-house (kegchreon)," instead of "in the cleansing-house," where they dried the millet-ore from the mines, as Theophrastus suggests in his work On Mines.
Keioi. Lysias in the speech On His Own Benefactions: "the Ceans, a city of such size." Ceos is one of the Cyclades islands, lying near Attica. The orator called the island a city. Euripides too called Euboea so: "Euboea is some neighboring city to Athens." And Aristophanes, concerning Sicily, says: "what a wretched city is being utterly ruined."
Keiriades. Isaeus in the appeal Against Boeotus from the demesmen. That Ceiriadae is a deme of the tribe Hippothontis, Diodorus has said in his work On the Demes.
Kekropis. Hyperides in the speech Against Aristogiton. Cecropis was one of the ten tribes at Athens, as Demosthenes says in the Funeral Oration, if it is genuine.
Keleontes ("loom-posts"). Antiphon, in his Defense Against the Indictment of Demosthenes: "where he fixed the loom-posts (keleontes)." Properly the "keleontes" are the loom-uprights, as is clear in Aristophanes the comic poet. But here the orator would use it metaphorically for the upright timbers.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Kerameis. Hyperides in his speech On Behalf of Xenophilus, book one. Cerameis is a deme of the tribe Acamantis, as Diodorus says. Philochorus, in his third book, says these got their name from the potter's craft (keramike techne) and from sacrificing to a certain hero Ceramus.
Kerameikos. Antiphon in the speech Against Nicocles, Concerning Boundaries. That there are two Cerameici, as the orator too says—one within the city, the other outside, where they buried at public expense those who died in war and delivered the funeral orations—Callicrates or Menecles makes clear in the work On Athens.
Kerkidas. Demosthenes, in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon, listing the traitors, says "Cercidas of Arcadia." That this man was among those who favored Macedonian interests, Theopompus too has said in the fifteenth book of the Philippics.
Kerkouros. A kind of ship; Dinarchus in the Tyrrhenian speech.
Kerkops ("Cercops"). Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. In the poems ascribed to Homer, in the Cercopes, it is shown that the Cercopes were deceivers and liars. Xenagoras says they were changed into apes, and that the Pithecusae islands were named after them. Aeschrion of Samos, in his iambics, even records their names, Candulus and Atlantus.
Keineas. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is agreed among the historians too that Cineas was one of those who betrayed the affairs of the Thessalians to Philip, and especially by Theopompus in his first book, who at the same time describes the man's character.
Kersobleptes. The orators often mention this man, as also Demosthenes Against Aristocrates. He was a son of Cotys, and being very young was established by his father as king of Thrace. That he once made war on the Athenians concerning the Chersonese, Isocrates too makes clear in the speech On the Peace.
Kestrinoi. Hyperides in the speech On the Salt-Fish. The "kestrinos" is a fish. But one must consider whether it differs at all from the "kestreus" (mullet).
Kefalos. A proper name, a demagogue.
Kefalethen ("from Cephale"). Isaeus in the speech Against Calydon Concerning a Guardianship. Cephale is a deme of the tribe Acamantis, from which the demesman is said to be "from Cephale" (Kephalethen), as Diodorus says.
Kedonides. Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus: "passing over these savage men, Cedonides and Autocleides and Thersander." These were violent lovers of boys.
Kekis ("gall-dye"). A certain dye and astringent, or a fruit of the oak suitable for dyeing; Demosthenes in his speech Against Aphobus, book one.
Kepos ("garden"). Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. There is a city on the Bosporus called Cepos ("Garden").
Kerukeia ("herald's fee"). The pay given to the heralds at the sales that take place; Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes.
Kerukes ("the Heralds"). Isocrates in the Panegyricus. There is a clan at Athens so named; it was called after Ceryx the son of Hermes.
Kettoi. Lysias in the speech Against Nicides for Idleness. It is a deme of the tribe Leontis, as Diodorus the geographer says.
Kefisieus. Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes. It is a deme of the tribe Erechtheis, as he himself says.
Kefisodoros. Lycurgus in the speech Against Menesaechmus. This man was ridiculed in comedy as sluggish. There is another Cephisodorus who, being a cavalry-commander, died at Mantinea together with Gryllus the son of Xenophon, whom Dinarchus mentions in the speech Against Callaeschrus.
Kefisodotos. Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. Androtion, in the fifth book of his Atthis, relates that, while besieging Alopeconnesus, he was deposed by show of hands, and being tried was convicted and paid five talents.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Kigklis ("lattice-gate"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristogiton. The doors of the law-courts were called "lattice-gates" (kigklides); Aristophanes in the Banqueters: "and the juror crept toward the lattice-gate."
Kinados ("beast"). Used instead of "wild beast" by Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is found in comedy too, as in Aristophanes. They say that the Sicilians, in a special sense, call the fox "kinadion."
Kinesias. There are two speeches of Lysias Against Cinesias, in which he often mentions the man, saying that he was most impious and most lawless, and that the comic poets write against him every year. This would be the dithyramb-poet, whom the comic poets often mention, and Strattis, who composed a whole play against him, entitled Cinesias, in which he also makes comedy of his impiety.
Kirraion pedion ("the Cirrhaean plain"). Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. Cirrha is a city distant thirty stades from Delphi. The orator seems, then, to call "Cirrhaean plain" the plain lying beside this city.
Kisthene. Isocrates in the Panegyricus. A mountain of Thrace. Cratinus: "and thence you will come to the ends of the earth and see the mountain Cisthene."
Kittoforos ("ivy-bearer"). Some write it with a sigma, "kistophoros" ("chest-bearer"); for they said that the so-called chests (kistai) were sacred to Dionysus and to the two goddesses.
Klimazei. Dinarchus, in the work entitled A Speech in Support of Aeschines Against Dinias: "whenever, then, in his defense he 'klimazei' and distorts the laws," instead of "bends aside and perverts." Perhaps one should write "blimazei," so that it means "presses hard and forces."
Klerouchoi ("cleruchs"). Demosthenes in the eighth book of the Philippics. "Cleruchs" were those whom the Athenians sent to the cities they took, distributing allotments (kleroi) to each. Isocrates in the Panegyricus: "for which the right-minded ought to feel great gratitude, far rather than to reproach us for the cleruchies, which we sent out to the depopulated cities for the sake of guarding the territory, and not through greed." But in the speech On the Symmories Demosthenes would mean by "cleruchic property" the property of those sent out to some other land under a cleruchy; "for how can a man not residing at Athens serve as trierarch?"
Klesis ("summons"). The summons, that is, the citation to trial; Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. That they also said "prokleseis," the same author makes clear in the speech Concerning the Estate of Hagnias.
Kleteres ("summons-witnesses"). Kleteres and kleteuein: the "kleteres" are the men through whom those bringing suits against others summon them to the trials; for there had to be present certain persons, as it were witnesses, of the summons; Isaeus in the speech Against Neocles, Concerning a Plot of Land. The word is altogether frequent both among the orators and in the old comedy. "Kleteusai" is to become a summons-witness, as Isaeus says in the speech Against Cleomedon. But "to be summoned" and "to be called out" are also used of witnesses, when they do not respond to give testimony in the courts; and there is a penalty against them of a thousand drachmas, as Isaeus says in the speech On Behalf of Python for Desertion.
Kobaleia ("knavery"). Dinarchus in the information Against Pytheas. "Kobaleia" was the term for pretended jesting with deceit, and "kobalos" the man who used it. It seems synonymous with "bomolochos." Philochorus, in the second book of his Atthis: "for one must not, as some say, suppose Dionysus to be a buffoon and a knave (kobalos)." Aristotle, in the eighth book of the History of Animals, says that the eagle-owl is a knave (kobalos) and a mimic, and is caught while dancing in answer.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Koinon grammateion ("common register"). Koinon grammateion and lexiarchikon: the "common register" is the one in which were enrolled those introduced to the phratry-members and clansmen; the "lexiarchikon" is the one in which were enrolled those registered in the demes, as other orators show and Isaeus in the speech Concerning the Estate of Apollodorus.
Koinonikon ("partnership property"). Demosthenes in the speech On the Symmories. By "partners" (koinonikoi) he would perhaps mean brothers having undivided property, whose father could perform public services, but whose heirs, taking the property singly, were not sufficient each to serve as trierarch; or perhaps also those who had agreed on a voluntary partnership in trade or some other matter, of whom each did not have the whole assessment of the common property.
Koironidai. There is a speech of Lycurgus entitled The Adjudication of the Croconidae against the Coeronidae, which some think to be by Philinus. The Coeronidae are a clan, about whom Ister speaks in his Collection of the Atthis. It would have been named after Coeron, whom they say was the bastard brother of Crocon, on which account the Croconidae are more honored. But the author of the speech, whoever he is, says they were called by three names: Coeronidae and Philieis and Perithoidae.
Kolluteus. Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus. Collytus is a deme of the tribe Aegeis.
Kolonetas. Hyperides, in the speech Against Apellaeus, Concerning the Treasure. They named the hired men "Colonetae," since they stood by the Colonus, which is near the marketplace, where the Hephaesteum and the Eurysaceum are; and this Colonus was called "of the marketplace." There was another Colonus by the shrine of Poseidon, as Hyperides says in the speech Against Autocles; this would be the Colonus "of the knights." Pherecrates in the Petale: "where do you come from, fellow? I was hurrying to Colonus. Not the one of the marketplace, but the one of the knights." Demosthenes, in the speech On the . . . , says "from Colonus." Concerning the Coloni, Diodorus the geographer and Philochorus in the third book of his Atthis have treated.
Komistika ploia ("transport vessels"). Hyperides, in the speech Concerning the Guarding of the Tyrrhenians. The "transport vessels" seem to be those in which the Tyrrhenians carried the spoils they had taken, as the orator himself suggests in the speech.
Kommata ("husks"). Kommata and kyrebia: Dinarchus in the information Against Callisthenes. The "kyrebia" are the bran; the "kommata" seem to be certain parts either of the straw or of the things about the grain itself in the ear, or of the beards of grain.
Kordakismos ("the cordax-dance"). Demosthenes in the Philippics. The "cordax" is a kind of comic dance, as Aristoxenus says in his work On Tragic Dancing. The word is found in the old comedy too, as in Nicophon.
Koroplathos ("doll-moulder"). Isocrates, in the speech On the Exchange of Property. They so named those who moulded girls or boys out of clay or wax or some such material.
Korsiai. Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines. Corsiae is a city of Boeotia, as Theopompus says in his thirtieth book.
Kotulaion oros ("Mount Cotylaeum"). Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. It seems to be a mountain of Euboea; at any rate Archemachus, in the third book of his Euboean History, says: "Cotylus, then, appears to have held the mountain now called Cotylaeum after him."
Kotus. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. This man ruled Thrace for twenty-four years; at first he lived in luxury and indulgence, but afterward, as his prosperity increased, he was carried away into savagery and rage, so that he even cut his wife, by whom he had children, in two with his own hands, beginning from the genitals.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Krauallidai. Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. Didymus says it should be written "Craugallidae"; for so was called the territory in Phocis near Cirrha, the "Craugallium," as Xenagoras too relates in the fourth book of his Chronicles.
Krastis. Dinarchus in the speech Against Lysicrates. "Krastis" is grass, as Aristophanes too says.
Krithoten. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aristocrates. Crithote is one of the cities in the Chersonese, as Hellanicus says in the first book of his Trojan History. But Ephorus, in his fourth book, says it was settled by the Athenians who came there with Miltiades.
Krioeus. Demosthenes in the speech Against Phaenippus. Crioa is a deme of the tribe Antiochis, as Diodorus says in his work On the Demes.
Krobulos. Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. Hegesippus is the one surnamed Crobylus; but properly the "krobylos" is a kind of hair-knot, as Thucydides says in his first book.
Ktesiou Dios ("of Zeus Ctesius"). Hyperides in the speech Against Apellaeus. They set up Zeus Ctesius ("of property") in the storerooms; Menander in the False Heracles: "but now, when I see a parasite going into the women's quarters, and Zeus Ctesius keeping the storeroom unlocked but with little harlots running in."
Ktesifon. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aeschines: "for at the outset, until Philip obtained a hearing concerning the peace, Ctesiphon and Aristodemus bore the first share of the deception." This man was one of the ten envoys who served on embassy with Demosthenes and Aeschines; each of the orators, at any rate, often mentions him in the speech On the Embassy. There would be another man, the one who proposed the decree about the crown for Demosthenes, against whom Aeschines' speech Against Ctesiphon is directed.
Kudathenaieus. Hyperides in the speech Concerning the Estate of the Knight. Cydathenaeon is a deme of the tribe Pandionis, from which the demesman is Cydathenaeus.
Kudantides. Hyperides in the speech Against Polyeuctus. Cydantidae is a deme of the tribe Aegeis.
Kutherios. Demosthenes in the speech Against Phaenippus. Cytherus is a deme of the tribe Pandionis, from which the demesman is called Cytherius.
Kuthnioi. Demosthenes in the speech On the Levy. Cythnos is one of the Cyclades islands, as Aristotle says in the Constitution of the Cythnians.
Kukloi ("the circles"). Dinarchus in the speech Against Callaeschrus. "Circles" were the places in which certain persons were sold; they were named from the fact that those being sold stood round in a circle. Menander in the Ephesian: "I think now, by the gods, that I see myself stripped in the circles, running round in a circle and being sold."
Kumbion ("the cymbium-cup"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Meidias. The "kymbion" is a kind of drinking-cup. Didymus says it is long and narrow and similar in shape to the boat called a "kymbion."
Kunnidai. Lycurgus in the adjudication of the Croconidae against the Coeronidae. The Cynnidae are a clan among the Athenians.
Kunosarges. Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates. The Cynosarges is one of the gymnasia among the Athenians.
Kuprothemis. A proper name. Demosthenes in the speech On the Freedom of the Rhodians: "Samos, garrisoned by Cyprothemis, whom Tigranes the king's viceroy installed."
Kupassis. Lysias in the speech On Behalf of Bacchius and Pythagoras, if it is genuine. The glossographers say the "kypassis" is a kind of tunic, some saying a woman's, others a man's. Hipponax mentions it, and Hecataeus in his Description of Europe, saying: "the Cissians wear Persian tunics (kypasseis)"; and Aristophanes in the Frying-pan Men.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Kurbeis. Lycurgus in the speech Concerning the Priestess. The "kyrbeis," Apollodorus says in his work On the Gods, have the laws inscribed on them, and they are upright standing stones, which from their standing they called "stelae," but from their upward extension, because they were brought to a point (kekoryphosthai), they called "kyrbeis," just as they called the headdress placed on the head a "kyrbasia." Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says: "having inscribed the laws on the kyrbeis, they set them up in the Royal Stoa."
Kureion ("the Cyrean army"). Isocrates in the Panegyricus. The "Cyrean army" is the one that marched up with Cyrus, when he campaigned against his brother Artaxerxes; in which Xenophon too took part.
Kurebion. Demosthenes in his speech Against Aeschines. That this is a nickname of Epicrates, the brother-in-law of Aeschines, has been shown elsewhere too.
Kuria ekklesia ("sovereign assembly"). Hyperides in the speech Against Demeas for Alien Status, if it is genuine. What the "sovereign assemblies" are, Aristotle has shown in the Constitution of the Athenians, saying that the prytaneis convene the Council and the people—the Council daily, except when there is a holiday, and the people four times in each prytany. He says they announce in advance a "sovereign assembly," in which the magistrates who seem not to govern well must be confirmed or removed by show of hands, and matters concerning the guarding of the territory are dealt with. And he says that on this day those who wish make their impeachments, and so on.
Kursilon. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "having chosen as general Themistocles, who gave this counsel, but stoning to death Cyrsilus, who declared that they should submit."
Kodeia ("poppy-head"). They so call the head of the poppy; Hyperides, and Aristophanes in the Farmers: "a good poppy-head."
Kolias. Demosthenes in his speech Against Neaera, if it is genuine. Colias is a coastal headland of Attica, named by metaphor from the "kolon" (limb); there is there a shrine of Aphrodite. Aristophanes mentions it at the beginning of the Lysistrata.
11. Lagiska. Lysias in the speech Against Lais, if it is genuine. Lagisca the courtesan is mentioned by Strattis the comic poet too, thus: "to see Lagisca, the concubine of Isocrates, while she was still gathering figs in bed, and the flute-bore himself."
Lampadion ("little torch"). What we now call a "lampas" (torch) they used to name thus; Dinarchus in the speech Against Pytheas, and Plato in the first book of the Republic.
Lampas ("torch-race"). Lysias in the speech Against Euphemus. The Athenians hold three torch-festivals: at the Panathenaea, the Hephaestia, and the Promethia, as Polemon says in his work On the Tablets in the Propylaea. But Ister, in the first book of his Atthis, having said that at the festival of the Apaturia the Athenians who have put on the finest robes take kindled torches from the hearth and run, singing the praise of Hephaestus—a memorial of the man who, having understood the use of fire, taught it to the others.
Lamptreis. Demosthenes in the speech Against Callippus. Lamptrae is a deme of the tribe Erechtheis, as Diodorus says. There are two Lamptrae, the coastal and the upper; Aristophanes in the Amphiaraus: "I am a Lamptraean of the lower deme."
Larkos. Lysias in the speech Against Callippides. The "larkos" is a basket into which they put charcoal. Others use the word, and Aristophanes in the Acharnians.
Laruggizein ("to bawl"). To broaden the voice and not to utter naturally, but to make an over-elaborate use of the throat (larynx), was so called; Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Lebadeia. Lycurgus in the speech Against Lysicles. It is a city of Boeotia.
Lembos. Demosthenes in the speech Against Zenothemis. The "lembos" is a kind of ship; it is often mentioned in comedy.
Leschai ("lounges"). Antiphon in the speech Against Nicocles. They called certain public places "leschai," in which many sat at leisure. Homer: "nor are you willing to go and sleep in the smithy or in the lounge." Cleanthes, in his work On the Gods, says that the "leschai" are assigned to Apollo, and that they are like exedrae, and that among some the god is surnamed "Leschenorios."
Leukas. Demosthenes in the eighth book of the Philippics. It is an island lying off Epirus.
Leuke ("the white poplar"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "crowned with fennel and white poplar." Those initiated into the Bacchic rites are crowned with white poplar, because the plant is of the underworld, and Dionysus the son of Persephone is also of the underworld. They say the white poplar grew by the Acheron, whence it is also called "Acherois" in Homer: "he fell as when some oak falls, or a poplar, or a tall pine."
Leuke akte ("White Cape"). Lysias in the speech Against Alcibiades. There being several White Capes, as Demetrius of Magnesia shows, the orator seems now to mean the one in the Propontis.
Leukonoieus. Demosthenes in the speech Against Aphobus. Leuconoion is a deme of the tribe Leontis, as Diodorus says.
Leuktra. Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is a Boeotian place near Thespiae.
Lechaion. In his Defense on the Indictment of Mixidemus, Lysias says that Lechaeum was captured in the archonship of Mnasippus. Lechaeum is the harbor-town of the Corinthians.
Leokoreion. Demosthenes in his speech Against Conon. The Leocoreum, Phanodemus says in the ninth book of his Atthis, is in the middle of the Cerameicus.
Lexiarchikon grammateion ("the deme-register"). Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus: the register into which were enrolled those of the boys who had come of age, to whom it was now permitted to manage their patrimony, whence too the name came, from their having authority over "lexeis"; and "lexeis" are the estates and properties, as Dinarchus too says in his first speech in support of Hegelochus, concerning an heiress.
Lexis ("claim"). The charge, in the sense in which we also say "to obtain a suit by lot"; Isaeus in the appeal Against Boeotus.
Lete. Hyperides Against Demades. Lete is a city of Macedonia, which Marsyas the younger often mentions in the sixth book of his Macedonian History.
Lithos ("the stone"). Demosthenes in his speech Against Conon: "leading us one by one, just so, to the stone and putting us on oath." The Athenians seem to have taken their oaths by a certain stone, as Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians and Philochorus in his third book suggest.
Liknoforos ("winnowing-basket-bearer"). Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. The winnowing-basket (liknon) is suitable for every rite and sacrifice; the one who carries it, then, would be called "liknophoros."
Lipara. Dinarchus in the Tyrrhenian speech. Lipara is one of the so-called islands of Aeolus near Sicily, as Eudoxus says in the seventh book of his Description.
Logismos ("calculation"). The art of reckoning; Isocrates in the Busiris.
Logistai ("auditors"). Logistai and logisteria: a magistracy among the Athenians so called; they are ten in number, who audit the accounts of those who have administered office within thirty days, when the magistrates lay down their offices; Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. Aristotle has discoursed about them in the Constitution of the Athenians, where it is shown that they differ from the "euthynoi." The comic poets too mention the office; Eupolis in the Cities: "auditors of the choruses subject to audit." "Logisteria" are the offices of the auditors, as Dinarchus shows in the speech Against Timocrates, and Andocides in the speech On the Mysteries.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
Logopoios ("story-writer"). What we call the historian; Isocrates in the Busiris, and Herodotus in his second book.
Logou tuchein ("to obtain mention"). Used instead of "praise" by Demosthenes in his speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon.
Loidias. Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. That it is a river of Macedonia, others relate, and Hecataeus in his Description of Europe.
Loutroforos ("the bath-bearer"). Loutrophoros and loutrophorein: it was a custom for those marrying to send for baths for themselves on the day of the wedding; and they sent for this the nearest male kinsman, and these "bore the bath" (eloutrophoroun). It was also a custom, when the unmarried died, to set a "loutrophoros" upon the tomb; this was a boy holding a water-jar. Dinarchus speaks of these things both in the speech Against Theodotus and in the information Against Callisthenes. That they fetched the baths from the spring now called Enneacrunus, formerly Callirrhoe, Philostephanus says in his work On Springs. The comic poets too mention the custom.
Lousieus. Hyperides in his speech on the indictment Against Demeas. Lousia is a deme of the tribe Oeneis, from which the demesman is Lousieus, as Diodorus says.
Lukeion. Demosthenes in his speech Against Timocrates. The Lyceum is one of the gymnasia among the Athenians, which Theopompus, in his twenty-first book, says Peisistratus made, but Philochorus, in his fourth book, says came to be while Pericles was overseer.
Lukiourgeis ("of Lycian workmanship"). Demosthenes in the speech Against Timotheus. Didymus says that the bowls made by Lycius, the son of Myron, were so called. But the grammarian seems not to know that one would not find such a formation made from proper names, but rather from cities and nations: Critias, in the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, says "a couch of Milesian workmanship (Milesiourges)." Perhaps, then, one ought to write also in Herodotus, in his seventh book, "Lycian-worked" (Lykiergeas) instead of "Lycurgus-worked" (Lykoergeas) javelins, so that, as in Demosthenes, the things wrought in Lycia might be so named.
Lukourgos. One of the ten orators, whose grandfather was Lycurgus the lawgiver.
Lusandros. A proper name, an admiral of the Lacedaemonians.
Lusimachos. Demosthenes in his speech On the Immunities. He was the son of Aristides, surnamed the Just. There is another Lysimachus whom Lycurgus mentions in the speech On the Administration, as a worthless lyric poet.
maimakterion. MAIMAKTERION
The fifth month among the Athenians; Demosthenes in the speech Against Timotheus. It is named after Zeus Maimaktes. A "maimaktes" is one who is impetuous and turbulent, as Lysimachides says in his work On the Months at Athens; for at the time when winter takes its beginning, in this month the air is disturbed and undergoes change.
makrokephaloi. MAKROKEPHALOI ("Long-heads")
Antiphon in the work On Concord. There is a people so called, whom Hesiod also mentions in the third book of the Catalogue of Women. Palaephatus, in the seventh book of his Trojan History, says that the Long-heads dwell in Libya, above the Colchians.
malkiomen. MALKIOMEN ("We grow numb")
Demosthenes in the ninth of the Philippics says, "we wait and grow soft." In some copies it is written "we grow numb," which means to shiver to the very base of the spine. Aeschylus: "Drive on, pursue with foot unwearied, though it grows numb."
malthe. MALTHE
Softened wax; Demosthenes in the speech Against Stephanus. Hipponax: "then having smeared the keel with wax."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
mantineon_dioikismos. THE BREAKING-UP OF MANTINEA INTO VILLAGES
Isocrates, in the speech On the Peace, speaking of the Lacedaemonians, says they "broke up Mantinea into villages"; and Ephorus in the twentieth book says that the Lacedaemonians broke up the city of the Mantineans into five villages.
margites. MARGITES
Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon: "and he gave Alexander the nickname Margites." And Marsyas, in the fifth book of his work On Alexander, records that Alexander was called Margites by Demosthenes. They used to call foolish men by this name, after the Margites attributed to Homer, a poem which Callimachus seems to have admired.
maroneia. MARONEIA
Demosthenes in the special plea against Pantaenetus. It is a place in Attica. There is also, however, a city in Thrace called Maroneia, which is said to be the one Homer calls Ismarus; Demosthenes mentions it in the speech Against Polycles, and Ephorus in his fourth book.
massalia. MASSALIA
Isocrates says, in the Archidamus, that the Phocaeans, fleeing the dominion of the Great King, migrated to Massalia; but that Massalia had already been settled by the Phocaeans before that time, Aristotle too makes clear in the Constitution of the Massaliots.
masteira. MASTEIRA
In the eighth of the Philippics Demosthenes says, "of the evils in Thrace—for what else could one call Drongilus and Cabyle and Masteira?" Perhaps one should write Basteira, or Pisteira, or Epimastus, since we find these cities in Anaximenes in the seventh book of his work On Philip, whereas Masteira is nowhere recorded.
masteres. MASTERES
Hyperides in the speech Against Pancalus. It seems to have been a magistracy established to investigate the public affairs of the people, like the inquisitors, and the "mastroi" at Pellene, as Aristotle says in the Constitution of the Pelleneans.
matruleion. MATRYLEION
Deinarchus in the speech Against Proxenus. Heracleon and Didymus say it is a certain place in which old women, lingering there, receive those who wish to drink themselves senseless. Menander in the Arbitrants: "Will he not come to grief, having ruined his life in a brothel?"
mausolos. MAUSOLUS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Timocrates. A proper name; a ruler of the Carians. Theopompus says of him that he abstained from no act for the sake of money.
machatas. MACHATAS
A proper name.
medimnos. MEDIMNUS
Deinarchus in the speech Against Callisthenes. It is a measure of dry goods, such as wheat or barley, and contains forty-eight choenixes, as Nicander of Thyateira says in his works expounding the Attic dialect.
methone. METHONE
Demosthenes in the Philippics. He would mean the Methone in Thrace, in besieging which Philip had his right eye struck out. But Demetrius of Magnesia, in his work On Cities of the Same Name, says there are four Methones.
meion. MEION
MEION and MEIAGOGOS: Isaeus in the speech Against Stratocles: "he presented a meion." It is a victim which those who introduced their children to the phratry-members offered to them. Eratosthenes, in his works On Comedy, says that, since there was a law not to introduce a victim below a fixed weight, in mockery and jest people used to say that anyone who introduced a victim "introduced a meion" ("a smaller one"), whence the sacrificial animal was called "meion," and the one who introduced it "meiagogos." Apollodorus, in his work On the Gods, says: the phratry-members, in order to receive larger portions, used to cry out, as they stood there, that it must be set up to weigh, for it is "a meion" (too small). Concerning the "meiagogos," Eupolis in the Demes: "Therefore from that time on no general was able, like a meiagogos feasting them, to draw a weight greater than the victory of this man."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
meiagogesai_de_esti. MEIAGOGESAI: it is
MEIAGOGESAI means to deliver the meion to the phratry-members, as Lysias has it in the speech Against Demosthenes concerning a guardianship.
melanippeion. MELANIPPEION
Lycurgus in the speech Against Lycophron. It is a hero-shrine of Melanippus the son of Theseus, as Asclepiades says in the Subjects of Tragedy. But Cleidemus, in the first book of the Atthis, says it is in Melite.
melanopos. MELANOPUS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Androtion. A proper name; the father-in-law of Diophantus the orator.
meline. MELINE ("Millet")
Demosthenes in the Philippics. It is the seed of a pulse, and they use the word as masculine; but Sophocles in the Triptolemus uses it as feminine: "shin of millet," and Herodotus: "sowing millet." Xenophon in the first book of the Anabasis: "both of grain and of millet," and in the same work: "much sesame and millet-oil," and in the sixth book: "and all kinds of pulse and millet." Now some consider millet to be a kind of panic-grass, which some call "elymos"; but Theophrastus, in the eighth book On Plants, records these as differing things—panic-grass, or millet, or "elymos."
melite. MELITE
Demosthenes in the speech Against Conon. It is a deme of the tribe Cecropis. Philochorus, in his third book, says the deme was named after Melite, daughter (according to Hesiod) of Myrmex, but (according to Musaeus) of Dius the son of Apollo.
mende. MENDE
Demosthenes in the speech Against Lacritus. Mende is one of the cities in Pallene, settled by the Eretrians.
menelaos. MENELAUS
Demosthenes in the Philippics. The brother of Philip by the same father.
mesegguema. MESENGYEMA ("Money held in escrow")
The agreed sum of money placed with a man acting as middle surety for its repayment. And MESENGYESASTHAI means to do this, as Aeschines indicates in the speech Against Ctesiphon.
metageitnion. METAGEITNION
Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Xenippus. The second month among the Athenians is so called. In it they sacrifice to Apollo Metageitnios, as Lysimachides says in his work On the Months at Athens.
metalleis. METALLEIS ("Miners")
Lysias in the speech Against Diochares, if it is genuine. Those who work the mines are called "metalleis." There is also a play of Pherecrates called the Miners, which Eratosthenes, in the seventh book of his work On Old Comedy, says Nicomachus composed.
metapurgion. METAPYRGION
Lysias in the speech On His Own Public Services. The structure between the towers upon a wall was called a "metapyrgion." Thucydides too uses it often, as in the third book.
metoikion. METOIKION ("Resident-alien tax")
Hyperides in the speech Against Aristagora. A metic is one who, migrating from another city, settles in a second city, not staying for a short while as a foreign visitor, but having established his dwelling there. They paid each year twelve drachmas, which was called the metoikion, as Eubulus shows in the Plangon. And Isaeus, in the speech Against Elpagoras and Demophanes, indicates that the man paid twelve drachmas as the metoikion, and the woman six, and that while the son was paying, the mother did not pay; but when he was not paying, she paid herself. That slaves freed by their masters also paid the metoikion has been shown by others of the comic poets, including Aristomenes. Menander, in the Anatithemene and in the Twins, says that they paid, in addition to the twelve drachmas, a further three obols, perhaps to the tax-farmer. Metics who did not pay the metoikion were brought before the sellers, and if convicted were sold, as Demosthenes says in the speech Against Aristogeiton. They also used to put the metics aboard the ships, as the same orator shows in the Philippics. The comic poets used to call the metics "trough-bearers" (skapheis), since at the processions they carried the troughs.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
metoionisasthai. METOIONISASTHAI
For "to change a bad omen"; Deinarchus in the speech Against Demosthenes.
metronomoi. METRONOMOI ("Controllers of measures")
There is a magistracy at Athens, that of the controllers of measures, as Deinarchus says in the speech Against Callisthenes. They were ten in number, five for the Piraeus and five for the city; they had the oversight of seeing that the measures of those who sold were just, as Aristotle too shows in the Constitution of the Athenians.
metaulos. METAULOS
Lysias in the defence speech On the Murder of Eratosthenes. The "metaulos" is what is called the dirty courtyard, where the fowls were kept; Aristophanes in the Lemnian Women, and Menander in the Thais.
mekuberna. MECYBERNA
Hyperides in the speech Against Demades. Mecyberna is a city in Thrace, twenty stades distant from Olynthus.
melobios. MELOBIUS
Hyperides in the speech Against Autocles. He is one of the Thirty who held tyrannical power among the Athenians.
meuroion. METROON
Lycurgus in the speech Against Aristogeiton. They set up the laws, having inscribed them, in the Metroon; Deinarchus shows this in the speech Against Pytheas.
mikon. MICON
Lycurgus in the speech On the Priestess: "and they fined Micon the painter for depicting the Greeks too meanly."
molpis. MOLPIS
Lysias, in the speech On the Estate of Diogenes, says, "Molpis, one of the ten in the Piraeus." So under the Thirty there were ten men ruling in the Piraeus, one of whom was Molpis, as Androtion says in the third book of the Atthis.
moirokles. MOEROCLES
A proper name; a man of Salamis, one of those who took no obscure part in Athenian public life.
moirologchesai. MOEROLONCHESAI
For "to obtain one's portion"; Antiphon in the defence speech Against the Indictment of Callias.
mounuchia. MUNYCHIA
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. A place by the sea in Attica. Hellanicus, in the second book of the Atthis, says it was named after a certain Munychus, king, the son of Pantacles.
mountchion. MUNYCHION
Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Xenophilus. The tenth month among the Athenians is so called, and in this month they sacrifice to Artemis Munychia.
mousaios. MUSAEUS
Lysias, in the speech against the indictment of Mixidemus, if genuine: "and that he had two slave-boys in attendance, of whom he calls the one Musaeus and the other Hesiod." That the man on trial made a practice of so naming his servants is clear; but concerning Musaeus, Aristoxenus, in the Praxidamanteia, says that some have said the man was from Thrace, others that he was an autochthon from Eleusis. Others have spoken of him too, among them Glaucus.
moran. MORA
Demosthenes in the Philippics. Certain Laconian military formations are so called. Aristotle has discussed them in the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians. He says there are six divisions called "morae," and that all the Lacedaemonians are distributed into the morae. Xenophon, in the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, says: "each of the civic morae has one polemarch, four captains, eight commanders of fifty, and sixteen commanders of an enomotia."
mulothros. MYLOTHROS
One who owns a mill and works in it; Deinarchus in the speech Against Callisthenes, often. The word is also common among the comic poets.
murioi_en_megalei_polei. THE TEN THOUSAND IN MEGALOPOLIS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines. It is a common council of all the Arcadians, which the historians often mention. Aristotle too has discussed them in the common Constitution of the Arcadians, at the beginning of the book.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
murtanon. MYRTANON
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It was a fort in Thrace, as Marsyas the elder says in the seventh book of his Macedonian History, and Anaximenes in the Philippics.
murtis. MYRTIS
Demosthenes, in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon, listing those who betrayed each city, says, "of the Argives, Myrtis, Teledamus, Mnaseas." But Theopompus, in his fifty-first book, names Paseas and Amyrtaeus as the Argives who took Macedon's side. One must therefore consider whether these are scribal errors.
muson_leian. THE BOOTY OF THE MYSIANS
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is a proverb so spoken, which Demon, in the first book of his work On Proverbs, says took its origin from the neighbours and brigands who overran Mysia during the absence abroad of Telephus the king. The proverb is used by others, among them Strattis in the Medea and Simonides in his iambics.
nais. NAIS
A courtesan; Lysias in the speech Against Philonides, if genuine, and Aristophanes in the Gerytades. Perhaps too in the Plutus, where the comic poet says "Lais loves you, but not for your sake, Philonides," it should be written with an "n," "Nais."
nannion. NANNION
Hyperides in the speech Against Patrocles, if genuine. Apollodorus, in his work On Courtesans, says this courtesan was called "Goat" (Aix) because she devoured Thallus the shopkeeper—for that goats delight in young shoots (thallos) Sophocles too shows in the Shepherds: "for early, before any of the herdsmen could see, bringing freshly plucked shoots to the she-goats, I saw an army marching along the seaside headland." There is mention of her also in comedy. And Antiphanes the younger, in his work On Courtesans, says that Nannion was nicknamed "Proscenium" ("Stage-front"), because from the outside she seemed more shapely.
naukleros. NAUCLERUS ("Shipmaster / Tenement-keeper")
Hyperides, in the speech On the Salt-fish, uses the word not only as ordinary usage employs it, but also of the man who has rented a house or tenement-block for the purpose of collecting the rents, as the same orator shows in the speech Against Aristogeiton, and Sannyrion in the Laughter, and Diphilus in the Merchant.
naukrarika. NAUCRARIKA
Demosthenes in the speech Against Timocrates. Perhaps, however, it is better to read in the Attic copies "Naucratitica," so that it refers to a Naucratite ship or to Naucratites sailing aboard; for Naucratis was of old the trading-post of Egypt. But if it is "naucrarika," it would mean the affairs of the magistrates; for of old they called the magistrates "naucrari," as Herodotus too shows in his fifth book. And Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says: "They appointed demarchs having the same charge as the former naucrari."
nautodikai. NAUTODIKAI ("Sea-judges")
Lysias in the speech Against Alcibiades, if the speech is genuine. The "nautodikai" were a magistracy at Athens; Craterus at any rate, in the fourth book of the Decrees, says: "if anyone born of two foreign parents enrols in a phratry, any Athenian who wishes, of those who have a right of action, may prosecute him, and the case shall be entered on the last day of the month before the nautodikai." Aristophanes in the Banqueters: "having dyed him, I want suddenly to bring the foreigner before the nautodikai . . ."
neales. NEALES ("Freshly caught")
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aristogeiton, if genuine. The man recently caught was so described, by a metaphor drawn from fish.
nebrizon. NEBRIZON
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. Some take it of the celebrant putting on a fawnskin, or also girding those being initiated with fawnskins; others, of tearing fawns to pieces according to some unspeakable doctrine. The "nebrismos" is mentioned also in Arignote's work On the Mysteries.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
neelata. NEELATA ("Freshly ground meal")
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon, by ellipsis for "freshly ground barley-meal," that is, meal recently milled, which they would moisten with honey, throwing in raisins and green chickpeas, and distribute to those performing the rites. Some called it ambrosia, others "the blessed food."
nemeas_charadra. THE RAVINE OF NEMEA
Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. A certain place in the Peloponnese was so called; Ephorus, in his twenty-third book: "near the Ravine of Nemea."
nemeas_auletridos_mnemoneuei_upereides_en. HYPERIDES MENTIONS NEMEAS THE FLUTE-GIRL IN
Hyperides mentions Nemeas the flute-girl in the speech Against Patrocles, if genuine. But Polemon, in his work On the Acropolis, cites a decree by which it was forbidden at Athens to give to a female slave or freedwoman or prostitute or flute-girl the name of a quadrennial festival. It is worth puzzling, then, how the flute-girl came to be so named.
nemeseia. NEMESEIA
Demosthenes in the speech Against Spudias. Perhaps there was a festival of Nemesis, at which they performed the customary rites for the departed.
neon. NEON
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. Concerning this man's friendship with Philip, Theopompus gives an account in the second book of the Philippics.
neoria. NEORIA ("Dockyards")
NEORIA and NEOSOIKOI: Perhaps "neoria" is the whole place into which the triremes are hauled up and from which they are again launched, as Lycurgus indicates in the Account of His Public Acts and Andocides in the speech On the Peace, if the speech is genuine.
neosi. NEOS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines. It is a city in Phocis, which Herodotus in his eighth book calls Neon, but Androtion in the sixth book of the Atthis calls Neones.
nikaia. NICAEA
Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. It is a city of Locris, lying by the sea.
nikanor. NICANOR
Hyperides in the speech Against Demosthenes. There were three men named Nicanor: one the son of Balacrus, another the son of Parmenion, and a third a Stageirite by birth, whom the orator would now be mentioning.
nike_athena. NIKE ATHENA
Lycurgus in the speech On the Priestess. That a wingless statue of Athena Nike, holding a pomegranate in the right hand and a helmet in the left, was honoured among the Athenians, Heliodorus the guide has shown in the first book of his work On the Acropolis.
notheia. NOTHEIA ("The bastards' portion")
What is given to bastards out of the paternal estate is so called; it amounted to as much as a thousand drachmas. Lysias in the speech Against Calliphanes for usurpation of citizenship, if genuine; Isaeus in the speech Against Lysibius concerning an heiress. Aristophanes in the Birds: "And what if my father, dying, leaves me his property, the bastard's share? The law does not allow it." In what matters bastards were not allowed to share, Hyperides has shown in the second speech Against Aristagora. And Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aristocrates, says that they were enrolled in the Cynosarges.
nomofulakes. NOMOPHYLAKES ("Guardians of the laws")
A magistracy at Athens was so called, distinct from the Thesmothetae; Deinarchus in the speech Against Himeraeus and in the speech Against Pytheas. Philochorus, in his seventh book, has discussed various matters concerning them, including that they used to compel the magistrates to abide by the laws.
notion. NOTION
Lysias in the speech Against Mantias. That it is a place lying before the city of the Colophonians, Theopompus says in his fifteenth book.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
numfaion. NYMPHAEUM
Aeschines, in the speech Against Ctesiphon, speaks of the Nymphaeum in the Pontus. But Craterus, in the ninth book of the Decrees, says that the Nymphaeum paid a talent to the Athenians.
xenizein. XENIZEIN
Demosthenes in the appeal against Eubulides, often. Some take it to mean "to use a foreign idiom," but perhaps it would rather mean "to spend time abroad."
xenikon_en_korinthoi. THE MERCENARY FORCE AT CORINTH
Demosthenes in the Philippics, and Aristophanes in the Plutus. Conon first organized it; Iphicrates later took it over, and Chabrias; with it they cut to pieces the Lacedaemonian division, under the generalship of Iphicrates and Callias, as Androtion and Philochorus say.
xeniteuomenous. XENITEUOMENOUS ("Serving as mercenaries")
For "serving for pay"; the mercenaries are called "foreigners" (xenoi). Isocrates in the address To Philip and in one of the Letters to Philip. Antiphanes in the Euthydicus: "I served as a soldier, living abroad as a mercenary."
xeraloifein. XERALOIPHEIN ("To anoint dry")
Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus. They used "xeraloiphein" of anointing oneself without bathing, as Didymus says in the twenty-eighth book of his Tragic Vocabulary and Nicander in the eighteenth book On the Attic Dialect, adding that perhaps what the trainers call "to be rubbed down dry" was also so described. Sophocles in the Peleus: "anointing oneself dry through the folds of the garment."
xupetaiones. XYPETAIONES
Hyperides in the speech Against Archestratides. Xypete is a deme of the tribe Cecropis, from which the demesman is "Xypetaion," as Diodorus says.
xustis. XYSTIS
Lysias in the speech Against Nicodemus and Critobulus. The "xystis" is a woman's garment, embroidered, as other comic poets make clear, and Antiphanes in the Euploea: "the man dressed in embroideries as in a xystis." There is also a tragic costume so called, as Cratinus in the Seasons shows; and there is also an equestrian garment, as Aristophanes in the Clouds.
obolostatoi. OBOLOSTATAI ("Petty usurers")
For "they lend"; Lysias in the speech Against Nicides, if genuine. In the speech Against Lacrates, explaining it, he says: "not even if one were to reckon a far smaller interest than these petty usurers exact from the rest." They used to call moneylenders "obolostatai," as in Hyperides in the speech Against Polyeuctus and often in comedy.
hodos. HODOS ("Road")
Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aristocrates, says "or having cut him down on the road," for "in ambush and in waylaying." They say the Homeric phrase "or to go upon the road" is of this kind too. But if the first vowel is left unaspirated ("odos"), it means a step or threshold, as in Lysias in the speech Against Philip, if the speech is genuine.
othneios. OTHNEIOS ("Alien")
Isaeus in the speech Against Stratocles, for "belonging to another," as also in Plato in the first book of the Laws.
oiethen. OIETHEN
Isaeus in the speech Against Elpagoras. Oie is a deme of the tribe Pandionis, as Diodorus says; "Oiethen" is an adverb of place ("from Oie"). Philochorus, in his third book, records Oie as a daughter of Cephalus and the wife of Charops.
oikeos. OIKEOS
Lysias, in the speech Against Theomnestus, as if explaining the word, says that "oikeos" means "a servant."
oikema. OIKEMA
For "prison," Deinarchus in the Tyrrhenian speech and in the speech Against Posidippus; for "brothel," Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus.
oikiskoi. OIKISKOS
For "a certain small house," Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. The Attic writers used to call what we call a "fowl-house" an "oikiskos"; Aristophanes in the Storks, Metagenes in the Breezes. From these passages Didymus seems to go astray in expounding the Demosthenic phrase as well.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
oineis. OINEIS
Hyperides in the speech Against Aristogeiton. One of the ten tribes among the Athenians.
oinoe. OINOE
OINOE and OINAIOS: Hyperides in the speech Against Aristogeiton: "and they said they had heard at Oinoe that a battle had taken place." Oinoe is a deme of the tribe Hippothontis, near Eleutherae; another is of the tribe Aiantis, near Marathon; and from either deme the demesman is called "Oinaios." The orator would now be mentioning the one near Eleutherae, which Thucydides too mentions in his second book.
oion. OION
Isaeus in the speech On the Adoption. There are two demes in Attica spoken of in the neuter, called Oion. Philochorus, in his third book, says they were so named because they had no inhabited place at all, but were left solitary; for the ancients called "solitary" (monon) "oion." The Ceramic Oion belongs to the tribe Leontis, and the Decelean Oion to the tribe Hippothontis, as Diodorus says. The demesmen from either were called "from Oion" (ex Oiou). There were others, however, called "from Oie" (Oiethen), as said above.
oios_ei. OIOS EI
OIOS EI and OIOS TE EI: the phrase without "te" means "you wish" and "you have chosen"; the one with "te" means "you are able." Lysias used both in the speech Against Lysitheus, if genuine.
oisume. OISYME
Antiphon in the speech Against Laispodias. It is a city of Thrace, as others say, including Ephorus in his fourth book.
hoti_diamartanei_demosthenes_en. THAT DEMOSTHENES IS MISTAKEN IN
That Demosthenes is mistaken in the speech Against Neaera, when he says that the Plataeans were depicted in the Painted Stoa; for no one has said this, just as neither has Craterus in his collection of the decrees. THE LAW FROM BELOW: Demosthenes in the speech Against Aristocrates. Didymus says either that the orator means the Heliaea, because of the courts some were called "those above" and some "those below," or, on account of the form of the writing on the wooden tablets, which was written "as the ox plows" (boustrophedon), Demosthenes calls the law that begins from the left-hand side "the law from below"; for that the tablets and the wooden pillars were written boustrophedon, Euphorion has shown in the Apollodorus. Or because, as Anaximenes says in the Philippics, Ephialtes moved the tablets and the pillars down from the acropolis to the council-chamber and the agora.
hoti_exakischilia. THAT SIX THOUSAND
That the assessed value of Attica was six thousand talents. Demosthenes, in the speech On the Symmories, says: "but for us the assessed value of the land, providing a fund of eight thousand talents, will be heard." Either, then, this is a scribal error, or perhaps the orator overstates it, so that the city may seem to have a greater fund for the war against the King. For that the assessed value of Attica was six thousand talents he both says in what follows in the speech, when the matter is resolved, giving the reckoning of it in detail, and Philochorus shows in the tenth book of the Atthis.
oligoresete. OLIGORESETE ("You will disregard")
For "you will neglect," Demosthenes in the Philippics. "To disregard" (oligorein) means to have "little care" (oligen oran); and "little" here stands for "not even a little," as in the line "and Tydeus begot a son in little like himself"—and "ora" means care.
holoschoinoi. HOLOSCHOINOS
Aeschines in the speech On the Embassy. Theophrastus, in the fourth book On Plants, having said that there are three kinds of rush, says that the third, differing in size and fleshiness, is called "holoschoinos."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
homereuontas. HOMEREUONTAS ("Serving as hostages")
Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon, of the Lacedaemonians sent up to Alexander. Cleitarchus, in his fifth book, says the hostages given by the Lacedaemonians were fifty. Hostages (homeroi) are those given as a pledge of an agreement; for "homeresai" means "to make a compact": Homer, "a messenger came to me from my companions in agreement." But Theopompus says that among the ancients "homerein" meant "to follow"; those, then, given to follow up the things agreed are from this called hostages.
homeridai. HOMERIDAI
Isocrates in the Helen. The Homeridae are a clan in Chios, which Acusilaus in his third book, and Hellanicus in the Atlantis, say was named after the poet. But Seleucus, in the second book On Lives, says that Crates errs in supposing, in the Hieropoiiai, that the Homeridae are descendants of the poet; for they were named after the hostages (homeroi), since once the women of the Chians, driven mad at the Dionysia, came to blows with the men, and when they had given one another bridegrooms and brides as hostages they ceased, and their descendants are called Homeridae.
homoerkes. HOMOERKES
Deinarchus in the speech against the special plea of Callippus, for "under one enclosure," that is, within the same wall.
homose_ienai. HOMOSE IENAI ("To come to close quarters")
Hyperides, in the speech Against Athenogenes, says "but I wish to come to close grips with this argument," for "to set myself against it." It is said by a metaphor from going up against spears, that is, advancing from the opposite side to the same point and neither turning nor fleeing.
homou. HOMOU ("Together / nearly")
