Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Xenophilus. The Tyrmeidai are a deme of the tribe Oineis, as Diodorus says.
turtaios. TYRTAEUS
Lycurgus in the speech Against Leocrates. The poet of the elegies.
huakinthides. HYACINTHIDES
Lycurgus in the impeachment Against Lycophron. They are the daughters of Hyacinthus the Lacedaemonian.
hubadai. HYBADAE
Lysias in the speech On the Daughter of Onomacles. It is a deme of the tribe Leontis.
hugieia_athena. ATHENA HYGIEIA
Lycurgus in the speech On the Priestess. It is an epithet of Athena; for she is called both Hygieia (Health) and Nike (Victory) and Hippia (of horses) and Ergane (the Worker).
hupagousin. HYPAGOUSIN
For "they lead forward," Demosthenes in the Philippics.
huperbolos. HYPERBOLUS
Antiphon in the speech Against Nicocles. He was a demagogue, whom Thucydides, in his eighth book, says was ostracized.
huperemeroi. HYPEREMEROI ("Defaulters")
Those who, having lost any suit and not paying the penalties to the winners within the appointed time-limits, were called "hyperemeroi," and the matter HYPEREMERIA, as Isaeus indicates in the speech Against Aristocles, if the speech is genuine.
hupo_gen_oikountes. THOSE DWELLING BENEATH THE EARTH
Antiphon in the work On Concord. He would mean those called by Scylax in the Circumnavigation "Troglodytes," and those named by Hesiod in the third book of the Catalogue "Underground-dwellers" (Katoudaioi).
hupokudeis_gar_eisin_oi_topoi. FOR THE PLACES ARE WATERY
Deinarchus in the speech Against Stephanus. "Hypokudes" means "moist through," as is clear from the third book of Ctesias. Euphorion: "as of a watery (hypokudes) water-meadow." In some of the copies, however, in the orator it is written "hypokoiloi" (hollow underneath).
hupologon. HYPOLOGON
Lysias in the speech On Abortion, if genuine, "not being reckoned (hypologon)," for "not taken into account." Deinarchus in the speech Against Pytheas: "no allowance has been made to the Council," for "no pardon, no excuse."
huponomeuontes. HYPONOMEUONTES
For "digging underground passages (hyponomoi)," Deinarchus in the speech Against Callippus.
hupostesas. HYPOSTESAS
For "having suborned," Hyperides in the speech Against Antias.
hupofonia. HYPOPHONIA ("Blood-money")
The moneys given on account of murder to the relatives of the slain, so that they may not prosecute; Deinarchus both in the speech Against Callisthenes and in the speech Against Phormisius, Theophrastus in the sixteenth book of the Laws.
hupomosia. HYPOMOSIA
The deferring of a suit on the plea of absence abroad or illness or some similar cause, on oath, was so called, and to do this was HYPOMNYSTHAI, as is clear both from other sources and from Demosthenes in the speech Against Olympiodorus.
husiai. HYSIAE
Hyperides in the speech On Behalf of Xenophilus. Hysiae is a city of Boeotia, which Euripides too mentions in the Antiope.
falaggia. PHALANGIA
Hyperides in the second speech Against Aristagora, that the "phalangion" is one of the biting creatures. Xenophon too makes this clear in the first book of the Memorabilia.

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
faleron. PHALERUM
Lysias in the speech Against Lysitheus. Phalerum is a deme of the tribe Antiochis, from which the demesman is "Phalereus."
fanias. PHANIAS
A proper name; one of those who had served as general.
fanostrate. PHANOSTRATE
Demosthenes in the speech Against Androtion. Apollodorus, in his work On the Courtesans at Athens, says she was nicknamed "Phtheiropyle" ("Louse-gate"), since, standing at the door, she would pick off her lice.
farmakos. PHARMAKOS ("Scapegoat")
Lysias in the speech Against Andocides for impiety, if genuine. They used to lead out two men at Athens to be purifications for the city at the Thargelia, one on behalf of the men, one on behalf of the women. That "Pharmacus" is also a proper name—and that, having stolen the sacred bowls of Apollo and being caught, he was stoned to death by the followers of Achilles, and that the rites performed at the Thargelia are imitations of these—Ister has said in the first book of the Epiphanies of Apollo. Since Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aristogeiton, says "this scapegoat (pharmakos), then, will get him off," Didymus thinks the word should be accented with the circumflex on the penultimate; but we have not found the usage so anywhere.
farmakonta. PHARMAKONTA
Demosthenes in the speech Against Stephanus. The "pharmakon" is the man harmed by drugs (pharmaka), as Theophrastus too indicates in the fifteenth book of the Laws.
fasis. PHASIS ("Information")
It is said both of a public charge, when someone informs that a person holds public property without having bought it, and also in the matter of orphans' estates. For when the guardians did not lease out the estate of their wards, anyone who wished informed against them before the archon, so that it might be leased; and he also informed if it had been leased for less than its worth. Of the former kind the testimonies may be found in Deinarchus and Demosthenes; of the information concerning orphans' estates, in Lysias in the speech "On the Information concerning an Orphan's Estate."
faskolon. PHASKOLON
A kind of pouch was so called among them; Isaeus and Lysias in the speech Against Dion, Aristophanes in the Women at the Thesmophoria.
faullos. PHAYLLUS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aristocrates. Onomarchus was tyrant of the Phocians; with him, while he lived, his brother Phayllus shared the rule.
fellea. PHELLEA
Isaeus in the speech On the Estate of Ciron. They called the rocky tracts, grazed by goats, "phelleae"; Cratinus in the Seasons, Aristophanes in the Clouds.
fegaieusi. PHEGAIEIS
Lysias in the speech On His Own Public Services. Phegaea is a deme of the tribe Aiantis, as Diodorus says.
felomata. PHELOMATA
Antiphon in the work On Concord: "deceptions"; for "to phelo" is to deceive.
fegousion. PHEGUSIUM
Lysias in the speech On the Murder of Batrachus. Phegus is a deme of the tribe Erechtheis.
fthoen. PHTHOE
Demosthenes in the speech Concerning the Children of Lycurgus, and Isocrates in the Aeginetic speech. What is now called "phthisis" (consumption) they called "phthoe."
filammon. PHILAMMON
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon: "Philammon the Athenian boxer."
filepsios. PHILEPSIUS
Demosthenes in the speech Against Timocrates. The poets of the Old Comedy mention Philepsius for telling tales between the public speeches; he is also satirized for knavery.
filiskos. PHILISCUS
Demosthenes. A proper name.
filosofein. PHILOSOPHEIN
For "to labour and to train," Isocrates in the speech On the Peace. Menander in the Thrasyleon: "he philosophizes about this, how he may accomplish the marriage."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
filotesia. PHILOTESIA
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines. The cup which they drank to their friends in friendship was called "philotesia," as Hyperides says, and Alexis.
fimoi. PHIMOI
Aeschines in the speech Against Timarchus: "and dice-boxes and other gaming implements." The "phimos" is what is called the "kemos" (funnel), into which the dice were thrown, as the glossographers say. Diphilus in the Synoris: "draw the dice-box into the middle, so that he may throw."
fluea. PHLYA
Isaeus in the speech On the Estate of Ciron. Phlya is a deme of the tribe Cecropis. From this deme was Euripides the tragic poet.
forbanteion. PHORBANTEION
Hyperides in the speech Against Patrocles. That the Phorbanteion at Athens was named after Phorbas, who reigned over the Curetes and was slain by Erechtheus, Andron has shown in the eighth book of the Kinships; and Phorbas was a son of Poseidon, as Hellanicus says in the first book of the Atthis.
forine. PHORINE
Antiphon in the second book of the Truth. That "phorine" (hide) was said also of human skin, Aristomenes in the Sorcerers makes clear.
frateres. PHRATERES
Demosthenes in the speech On the Name. The "phratry" is the third part of a tribe, and the "phrateres" are those sharing in the same phratry, and PHRATRIZEIN is to share in the same phratry; the PHRATRIARCHOS is the ruler of the phratry.
frearrios. PHREARRHIUS
Demosthenes in the speech On Behalf of Ctesiphon. It is a deme of the tribe Leontis.
froudos. PHROUDOS
Antiphon in the speech On the Murder of Herodes, for "gone away." The word is common among many writers.
fruktoron. PHRYKTOROI
"Phryktorein" properly means to signal anything by beacon-fires held aloft; Deinarchus in the speech supporting Aeschines against Deinias.
frunondas. PHRYNONDAS
Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. He was notorious among the Athenians for villainy, no less than Eurybatus.
frunon. PHRYNON
Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines. This man was one of the ten ambassadors, those who went with Aeschines and Demosthenes.
fularchos. PHYLARCHUS
Demosthenes in the Philippics. The "phylarch" is the commander of the cavalry of each tribe, subordinate to the hipparch, as Aristotle says in the Constitution of the Athenians.
fule. PHYLE
Isocrates in the speech On the Peace. Phyle is a deme of the tribe Oineis; Menander in the Dyscolus: "they hold the place to be Phyle of Attica, and the Nymphaeum, whence I come, belongs to the Phylasians." Philochorus, in the seventh book of the Atthis, says it is a fortress.
charaka. CHARAX ("Palisade")
Demosthenes. The palisade which some throw around a camp for safety. Menander in the Aspis: "for many, having abandoned the palisade, plundered the villages."
chalkeia. CHALKEIA
Hyperides in the speech Against Demeas for usurpation of citizenship. The Chalkeia is a festival among the Athenians held for Athena on the last day of Pyanepsion, common to all craftsmen but especially to bronzeworkers, as Apollonius of Acharnae says. But Phanodemus says the festival is held not for Athena but for Hephaestus. There is also a play of Menander called Chalkeia.
charikles. CHARICLES
One of the Thirty; Lysias.
chernibon. CHERNIBON ("Lustral waters")
Demosthenes in the speech Against Androtion: "and about to touch the lustral waters and the baskets." It would be from the nominative "chernips," the genitive plural "chernibon"; for the comic poets too mention the "chernips" as employed in the sacrifices. Aristophanes at any rate, in the Birds, says: "Boy, boy, take up the basket and the lustral water."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
chilioi_diakosioi. THE TWELVE HUNDRED
Isaeus, in the speech Against Ischomachus, says "no one named Lysides is among the twelve hundred." The wealthiest of the Athenians were twelve hundred, who performed the public services. Other orators mention them too, and Philochorus in his sixth book. But Lysias, in the speech Against Cleinias, and Isaeus, in the speech supporting Nicias, used the round number, saying "a thousand."
chiliothenta. CHILIOTHENTA
Lycurgus in the speech Against Aristogeiton, for "fined a thousand drachmas." The same orator, in the speech Against Cephisodotus, also says "to have been fined a thousand."
chilon. CHILON
A proper name; Aeschines.
chledos. CHLEDOS ("Rubbish")
Demosthenes in the speech Against Callicles concerning damage to land: "and then, having thrown the rubbish (chledos) into the road, by which it has come about that the same road is made higher and narrower." Any heap is called "chledos," and it is like a kind of pile, especially of sweepings and refuse, and the alluvial deposit of rivers, and still more of torrents, which is also called "cherados." Here the orator seems to mean that Callicles has thrown into the road a heap of earth and brushwood from the field, as he himself indicates in what follows. Many use the word. Aeschylus in the Argives: "casting both javelins and curved darts and rubbish."
choes. CHOES
Demosthenes in the speech On the Name. It was a festival held among the Athenians on the twelfth of Anthesterion. Apollodorus says that the whole festival held for Dionysus is called in common "Anthesteria," but in its parts "Pithoigia," "Choes," "Chytroi."
cholargeus. CHOLARGEUS
Isaeus in the speech On the Estate of Ciron. Cholargia is a deme of the tribe Acamantis.
cholleidai. CHOLLEIDAE
Lysias. A deme of the tribe Leontis.
chrestai. CHRESTAI
The word means two opposite things; for it means creditors, as in Isaeus in the speech Against Calydon and in Aristophanes in the Clouds—for he says "by harsh interest and most troublesome creditors I am hauled, I am carried off, my goods are taken in pledge"—and it is used of the borrower by others, including Demosthenes in the special plea On Behalf of Phormio. And in the special plea Against Zenothemis he says "but the lenders, deceived from the first, seeing that they had, instead of their money, a worthless debtor (chrestes) and nothing else."
chrusis. CHRYSIS
The bowl; Demosthenes in the speech Against Androtion, Aristophanes in the Peace.
chrusochoein. CHRYSOCHOEIN ("To smelt gold")
Deinarchus in the speech Against Pytheas: "for again, having gone off from Aeschines and studied under this man, he clearly was learning to smelt gold, but not to do or suffer the matter before him." Plato too uses the proverb, in the first book of the Republic, saying: "What? said Thrasymachus; do you think these men have now come here to smelt gold, and not to hear arguments?" They say the proverb arose from this: a rumour once fell among the Athenian multitude that on Hymettus much gold-dust had appeared and was being guarded by warlike ants. Taking up arms, they rushed out against them; but returning empty-handed, having toiled in vain, they mocked one another, saying, "And you thought you would smelt gold," which means, "you thought that, having gathered much gold-dust and smelted it, you would grow rich." They were ridiculed too by the comic poets; Eubulus at any rate, in the Glaucus, says: "we once persuaded the sons of Cecrops to take up arms and go out to Hymettus with three days' provisions against the ants, since gold-wrought dust had appeared."

title: Lexicon of the Ten Attic Orators
text:
chutroi. CHYTROI
Lysias in the speech Against Aeschines concerning the confiscation of the property of Aristophanes: "since, then, Demaratus was convicted of betraying Chytroi." It is a city in Cyprus so called, as Xenagoras says in the Islands. There is also a certain Attic festival, the Chytroi, which Deinarchus mentions in the speech Against Pytheas. The festival was held on the thirteenth of Anthesterion, as Philochorus says in his work On Festivals.
pseudeggrafe. PSEUDENGRAPHE ("False registration")
It is the name of a suit, which those entered as owing money to the public treasury bring in on the ground that the man who registered them has falsely entered them on the tablet placed beside the goddess, as having been unjustly registered as owing money to the treasury. Lycurgus in the speech Against Aristogeiton and Isaeus in the speech Against Medon mention the name.
pseudokleteia. PSEUDOKLETEIA ("False summons")
It is the name of a suit, which those entered as owing money to the public treasury bring in, when they charge that certain men have falsely produced witnesses to a summons against them, in regard to the suit through which they incurred the debt. It is found in other orators, and in Isaeus in the speech Against Nicocles concerning land.
psithuristes_ermes. WHISPERING HERMES
Demosthenes in the speech Against Neaera. There was at Athens a Hermes so called. There was also honoured at Athens a Whispering Aphrodite and a Whispering Eros.
